Depending on which bundle you pick up, you also might not have an “intimate comb” supplied with it, so I’d choose the Meridian Slimmer for a close trim below the belt.

Sources indicate that long-term testing notes: During three weeks with the 7000, it worked through my thick chest hair without pulling. Its slightly boxy handle was surprisingly comfortable around my underarms, with a textured grip that stayed secure at awkward angles. I also liked how well it handled facial hair, giving me a reason to keep one tool handy for several jobs. Esat Dedezade.

Sources indicate that while you might be able to get away with leaving your trimmer at home for a weekend by the shore, things have a way of unraveling fast over longer trips and vacations. For extended stays, you’ll want to pack a handy grooming companion to keep you tuned up from head to toe. The Lawn Mower 5.0 Ultra is designed to cross state lines and beyond: from the handy travel lock to keep the trimmer from powering on in your carry-on to the high-quality travel case to keep its attachments and charging cable organized.

The unique design of two adjustable length trimming guards allows each to be used to achieve three different lengths, which makes for easy transitioning and also saves space in the carry case. In our testing, the trimmer performed with reassuring power and accuracy. While 60 minutes is not the longest battery life, the trimmer’s constant RPM motor ensures the blade won’t slow down as battery levels dip. In any case, when it is time to charge, the Lawn Mower 5.0 Ultra supports USB-C and wireless charging. Adam Hurly.

If you’re ballin’ on a budget, Remington’s All-in-One Groomer is a capable, familiar trimmer that shouldn’t set off any fraud alerts on your credit card. Out of the box, this lightweight grooming tool is comfortable to hold, and the blade head twists into place with a satisfying click. The trimmer’s three fixed guards offer a standard spread of lengths, ranging from 3–9mm; and, for anything in between or beyond, the adjustable comb guard unlocks 10 additional length settings between 2–20mm. We were particularly impressed by the adjustable guard, which proved to be a handy tool for safely fine-tuning short to medium-length body hair with confidence. With additional attachments including a nose and ear trimmer, as well as a refined detail trimmer, the All-in-One Groomer lives up to its name, providing full-body coverage at an affordable price.

According to recent reports, won't settle for anything but the kind of hairless finish worthy of an Olympic swimmer? Philips' Body Groomer 5000 is the device pick up over a conventional trimmer. Its Triple Protect shaving system combines trimming and foil shaving, and there's also a separate trimmer head with adjustable combs covering 1–7mm. So you can leave some length on your chest or switch to the foil for a closer finish.

That head and comb arrangement differs from the British kit I reviewed, which had fixed guards and you’ll also need Philips’ own charging cable. It’s a familiar gripe when rival devices offer charging over UBS-C, but a small one next to how comfortably the shaving system worked for me.

Long-term testing notes: Over several weeks with the 5000, I used the cutters on either side of the foil to take down longer chest hair, then angled the foil against my skin to clear the stubble. Rushing through dense patches caused the occasional tug, but slowing down solved it. Below the belt, I got a smooth finish without cuts or irritation, and the light handle stayed comfortable through a longer session. All of which left me happy enough to put my wet razor away for a while. Esat Dedezade.

It has been revealed that shaving your own back is a time-honored chore for the hairiest among us, and the Mangroomer Intellimax Pro brings a home-inventor level of crazy brilliance to a job that otherwise requires extreme contortions. You just unfold it, power it on, drop it over the first shoulder, and get to mowing. The trimming head doesn’t bite or leave marks, but will take hair down to the normal .5mm, while the foil-head shaver attachment will get you smooth-skinned (for maybe a day or two). You can even adjust the length of the Mangroomer’s handle for taller torsos or to get better angles on tricky spots.

Sources indicate that it was a lifesaver for me when I was single (before I could sweetly ask my partner to do the job)—and so simple that shaving my back almost became fun. I would use it directly in the shower, making for easy cleanup. (Though never with the shower running; it's waterproof, but I didn't want the handle getting slippery enough that I’d drop it.) I never had any issues with nicking or razor burn with the Intellimax Pro’s main trimming head, though it was trickier to get a uniform shave using the foil shaving head. Frankly, it was easier to just use the .5mm trimming head every day if I wanted to stay stubble-free.

Sources indicate that the Slimmer’s compact head is its main attraction. There’s less machine to maneuver around tight spots, with two combs for leaving some length and a light for a better view – it stays off when you first switch the device on, and another press of the power button brings it into play. USB-C charging also saves you packing another cable. I just wish Meridian had included a pouch – with a trimmer this small and two loose combs, it feels like an obvious omission.

Its two combs cover 1.6mm or 4mm of hair length, so there’s some choice when you don’t want to take everything off. If you prefer longer chest hair, the longer guards on Meridian's Original model make more sense. Still, the Slimmer is the device I’d pick when close control over a blade matters most.

It has been revealed that long-term testing notes: I relied on the Slimmer for around a month on my chest and below the belt. The narrow head made awkward spots easier to navigate, and it cut through thick hair without pulling or nicking me. Without a comb, it left a hint of stubble I was happy with, although the Philips 5000’s foil gets smoother results. As for its ergonomics? The soft, grippy handle was comfortable, and the hinged blade made it easy to rinse out trapped hair. Esat Dedezade.

The OneBlade arrived on the scene years back as a hybrid between an electric trimmer/shaver and a manual razor, with replaceable cartridges ensuring you always had the sharpest cutting surface. The Intimate SkinProtect version steps up the game with coated teeth that protect against bites without compromising on stubble maintenance. For truly sensitive areas, I’d still recommend using the low-profile buffer guard to prevent friction or snips. And if you’re already a OneBlade owner, you can just buy the Intimate SkinProtect cartridges, and swap them on when you start working below the neck.

It has been revealed that right out of the box, the Black Ops inspires confidence with its well-weighted, stainless-steel build—wrapped in a grippy rubber handle to eliminate any chance of a slip. While it may sound like something you’d download for your PS5, the Manscaper Black Ops isn’t playing any games when it comes to getting the job done. The trimmer arrives with eight guards ranging from 1.5–13 millimeters, as well as an adjustable guide comb to give you more options for your hair down there. And, like its amphibious namesake, the Manscaper Black Ops is fully waterproof.

It has been revealed that we look for trimmers that can get through thick growth without pulling and are easy to control when we get to the awkward bits. We pay attention to how securely the guards fit, how comfortably the handle turns around the body, and how much work it takes to get a smooth finish. Cleaning, battery life, and charging matter, too, especially with a tool that may cover several grooming jobs.

It has been revealed that adam Hurly and Dean Stattmann bring their grooming reviews and health and wellness coverage to this guide, For this upgrade, Esat Dedezade has also drawn on his body-groomer testing for British GQ. The entries identify whose findings support each recommendation, and advice from celebrity groomer Dan Perri helps explain what to look for and how to maintain the tools.

What to Look For in a Body Hair Trimmer.

For a professional opinion on what to prioritize when buying an electric shaver or grooming kit, we sought out the expertise of celebrity groomer Dan Perri, who keeps A-list clients like Post Malone, Gerard Butler, and Brendan Fraser looking tidy. Here are the key attributes of a good body hair trimmer, says Perri:.

How do you maintain a body hair trimmer?

“If you want the best performance out of your trimmer, keeping the blade clean and lubricated is key,” indicates Perri. “Oiling the trimmer every few weeks will keep the blade running smooth, prevent any pulling of the hair, and keep the blade temperature down.” He adds that most trimmers come with a small supply of mineral oil—use it. (Wahl sells a great 4-oz clipper oil for cheap, too.) Be sure to use a machine-safe disinfectant spray to help keep the blade sanitized, which will prevent breakouts, Perri adds.

Can you use a beard trimmer for manscaping?

Industry observers note that some beard trimmers are designed for use on the body, but only if they have attachments designed to keep skin from being pulled into the blade. Keep in mind that the ergonomics of a great beard trimmer doesn’t necessarily align with the ergonomics you’ll want for shaving body parts. You’ll have a harder time hitting hard to reach places, like the back. And beyond that, you’ll want to aggressively sanitize any trimming heads and guards that touch both your face and your… [looks down].

What is the best body hair trimmer for men?

Recent findings suggest that we recommend the Philips Norelco All-in-One 7000 Series for most people who want to keep some length on their body hair. The 3mm and 5mm body combs let you choose how much to leave. For a smooth finish, go with the Body Groomer 5000 Series and its dedicated foil head.

How often should I trim my body hair?

Industry observers note that depends! If you want to be as smooth as an Olympic swimmer, you might want to shave every day. If that's too much of a hassle, doing it every two or three days can be sufficient to have you smooth without your stubble scratching up your shirts.

Should I shave off all of my body hair?

Do you find body hair unsightly? Then maybe you want to shave your body hair to give yourself a smoother appearance. The decision to trim body hair usually depends on what you or even your partner prefers. For professional sports, a hairless body might be preferred for an advantage, like for swimmers or wrestlers.

Is it better to trim body hair when it's wet or dry?

You can shave your hair whether it's wet or dry, but we prefer doing it on dry hair. Trimmers are able to more easily cut through the hair when it's dry, and you can get more even cuts if you're not going for a clean shave. (Though wet/dry trimmers are all over the market.).

What are common manscaping mistakes?

Besides using non-skinsafe grooming electricals (we got you covered in that department), some common manscaping mishaps are the result of poor technique (shaving against the grain), not trimming on cleansed, exfoliated skin, and neglecting post-shaving moisturizing—especially if you have sensitive skin.

According to recent reports, razor burn is no joke. Preparing the skin, using proper shaving technique, and including lotions, moisturizers, and other skin car products into you grooming routine are all good ways to prevent razor burn.

It has been revealed that dan Perri is a celebrity groomer based between NYC, LA, and Florida. His A-list clients include Post Malone, Gerard Butler, and Brendan Fraser.

  • More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a fresh personality. Unlike plain noodles, which promptly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Sources indicate that heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

It has been revealed that melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

On Wednesday, the Spanish monarch joined King Felipe VI and the Austrian president and first lady, Alexander Van der Bellen and Doris Schmidauer, to inaugurate the Mariana of Austria exhibition at Madrid’s Museo Nacional del Prado, before hosting a luncheon at Zarzuela Palace. Rather than changing outfits between engagements, Letizia switched out her shoes to produce quite a different effect.

Recent findings suggest that the queen opted for a burgundy pantsuit from Spanish label Bleis, comprising a single-breasted blazer and straight-leg pants, worn over a pink tie-neck blouse. She brought out the pink further by layering on a punchy, fuchsia Carolina Herrera felt coat that has been a firm favorite in her wardrobe for years.

She accessorized with a burgundy JW Pei Noor top-handle bag, pointed-toe Magrit kitten heels in a matching shade of leather, and zigzagging diamond earrings by Bárbara Goenaga, neatly rounding out her royal ensemble.

According to recent reports, come lunchtime, Letizia had traded her pointed pumps for a pair of pale pink patent Sézane Paula Babies: a rounded toe, double strap, and sturdy block heel shoe. The French label’s retro-inflected Mary Janes have become something of a wardrobe staple for the royal, who owns them in no fewer than five colorways. Her morning’s footwear emphasized the sharpness of her tailoring, while the second pair brought a sweeter sensibility to suiting.

Recent findings suggest that burgundy and pink proved itself a popular color combo on the fall 2026 runways, particularly at Chanel under Matthieu Blazy, with wider shades of red and pink at Celine. Queen Letizia has long had a knack for making the season’s more adventurous color trends work within the parameters of her royal wardrobe, too. Earlier this month, on a visit to Campus Diversia, she teamed a pair of navy corduroy pants with chocolate-brown outerwear and sturdy boots. Over the summer, she embraced yellow in a gathered Adolfo Domínguez dress flecked with other pastel shades. And who could forget her coronation weekend wardrobe all the way back 2023, when she went from a zesty green Victoria Beckham dress to a head-to-toe Barbie pink ensemble?

Sources indicate that what compounds the Spanish royal’s elegant sense of style is that so much of it is defined by pieces she’s had for years, reconfigured according to her schedule or the prevailing fashion mood. With a swift change of shoes or a refreshed color combo, you needn’t have the resources of a royal wardrobe to pull it off.

If your holiday spread always includes a plate of crispy latkes and a round of dirty martinis, these dirty martini latkes are probably your dream mash-up. This playful party app takes everything you love about the classic Hanukkah potato pancake and gives it a cocktail-inspired twist with buttery green olives, pimento peppers, and a tangy blue cheese and vermouth-spiked sour cream for dipping. The blue cheese isn’t mandatory, but if you love an ice-cold filthy martini with a couple of blue cheese stuffed olives in it, you’ll totally understand my vision. Pair these with other Hanukkah favorites for a festive spread that's equal parts nostalgic and fun.

Industry observers note that the latkes:Traditional latkes start with freshly grated potatoes, but frozen shredded hash browns are the secret shortcut here, cutting prep time without sacrificing crispy edges or fluffy centers. The key is squeezing out as much moisture as possible, then fluffing the shreds with a fork so they stay light instead of turning dense. Castelvetrano olives add a rich, buttery flavor, but Spanish queen or manzanilla olives work just as well. If you can find green olives already stuffed with pimento, go ahead and use them—you can skip the extra chopped pimentos altogether.

Industry observers note that make ahead & storage:The vermouth-blue cheese dipping sauce can be made up to 7 days ahead and stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator, making your day-of party prep that much easier. Leftover latkes can be refrigerated for up to 4 days; just reheat them in a 400° oven or air fryer until hot and crisp again for the best texture.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Power stations (i.e., solar generators) have become increasingly popular because they are easy to run, cost less over time than gas generators, and offer eco-friendly, emission-free operation, especially when paired with a solar panel. Some are small and compact, ideal for off-grid adventures, while larger ones are able to back up critical home circuits during a blackout.

Unlike fuel-based generators, solar generators can’t create electricity in real time. They’re giant battery packs, not true generators, and need to be recharged using alternating current (AC) power or solar panels, the latter of which often takes many hours in ideally sunny conditions.

Sources indicate that despite those distinctions compared to portable generators, there’s nothing more convenient than a power station for charging or running everything you need for day-to-day life—phones and laptops, lights, and even a small appliance or two. Plus, it’s nice to have a device that doesn’t produce carbon emissions and replenishes itself freely from the sun’s rays. Whether you’re seeking a highly portable option or need one that’s heavy-duty enough for extended use, these are the best solar generators we’ve tested and researched to date.

Industry observers note that to pick the best solar generators, we tested some of these power stations for charging capacity, ease of use, weight, and different use cases. Our picks were reviewed by Popular Mechanics editor Brad Ford, who provided input for the larger-capacity units. Other models on this list were reviewed by test editor David Dritsas or freelance writer Maggie Slepian.

Our primary concerns were portability and convenience. Ease of use was also important—was the display easy to read? Did the screen readouts make sense? Bonus points if we could tell how much power is available at a glance. In the past few years, these criteria have become easier to meet. There are now plenty of compact, affordable units that have better charging capabilities than before.

Very few power stations of this size can handle as much solar input power as the Bluetti Apex 200. With two input types—low-voltage XT60 (up to 1,000 watts) and high-voltage MC4 (up to 2,000 watts)—it can accept up to 3,000 watts of solar power. If you had the panels and ideal weather, you could fully charge this station in less than 2 hours—even faster than plugging it into the wall. That’s impressive.

Sources indicate that it also balances nicely between being a portable station and a home backup solution. It offers 3,200 watts of continuous power (it says 3,600 on the front, but that’s only if it’s connected to an expansion battery). We were able to power a refrigerator for a full 27 hours on a single charge, and estimated the battery efficiency at 90 percent, which is very good. Meanwhile, the 2,560-watt-hour battery capacity is expandable by adding up to six additional batteries. Using Bluetti’s largest battery, the B500K, you could build a massive 33-kilowatt-hour system.

While 3,600 watts isn’t enough to power a whole home, you could power a couple of circuits through a manual transfer switch using the 120-volt 30-amp output. But keep in mind that there’s no 240-volt support, so you can’t use it to power high-voltage appliances like electric dryers.

As a portable station, the Apex 200 has a lot to offer. At 59 pounds, it’s not too hard to move around the house or in and out of a vehicle. And there are several great DC power options, including a bank of USB outlets (two are high-power USB-C) and both 10- and 30-amp, 12-volt outputs. We also love that the AC ports can individually be turned on and off using the mobile app; this helps improve overall runtime.

Since very few stations can match its max solar input capacity, we concluded that the Apex 200 is definitely a top choice for anyone who wants a power station that can recharge using the sun’s rays, but also offers the versatility of being used on the road or at home.

Full Bluetti Apex 200 Power Station Review.

According to recent reports, this model replaces the original Jackery 1000, but many of the same observations made of the first model still apply. The new version has a slightly higher capacity of 1,070 watt-hours and uses a newer lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) battery, which is a newer battery technology that offers a longer lifespan (4,000 cycles versus 500 cycles for this model) and better performance in extreme temperatures.

In a recent development, expert Maggie Slepian used the previous model on a media trip where she had to keep multiple camera batteries charged during a weeklong outing. She found that while the capacity was lower than you'll find with others on this list, it actually powers items for longer than some higher-capacity models. She also charged her photographer’s camera batteries while charging the power bank on solar power (it was a very sunny winter day), which proved effective and efficient.

According to recent reports, the newer V2 model has seven ports, including three AC outlets, two USB-C ports (one 30-watt and one 100-watt), a 12-volt car port, and one standard 18-watt USB-A outlet. It charges a typical laptop eight times or powers a small refrigerator or an electric cooler for over 15 hours.

It has been revealed that the Jackery Explorer 1000 V2 charges with a 200-watt solar panel or a 12-volt outlet in your vehicle while you’re on the move. It has fairly standard charging times, with 11.5 hours in a car outlet, 6.5 hours for solar panels, and just 5.5 hours to fully charge in a wall outlet. This won’t be your best bet for powering larger appliances, but it’s an ideal power station for smaller items and off-grid camping.

Recent findings suggest that this power station takes solar recharging seriously. The Elite 300 can accept up to 1,200 watts of input, which is a high amount for a station this size. We paired it with a 250-watt portable panel and, on a fully sunny day, got around 260 watts of input. That’s the typical efficiency of a portable panel (again, you’ll never get 100 percent). But pair it with some larger panels, and you’ll get even more.

Sources indicate that it also boasts an impressive battery capacity of just over 3,000 watt-hours and 2,400 watts of output, which is high for a station of this size. Plus, it includes a 120-volt 30-amp port, which is handy for connecting it to a small RV or pop-up camper, allowing you to run small appliances and water pumps. It’s not enough power to run a heating or cooling system for a significant amount of time, but for lights, small appliances, and other items that need power, this station will deliver.

If there’s one downside we found, it’s that there’s no way to add an expansion battery to increase your capacity. That’s not a huge detractor, but it’s something we’ve seen in stations even smaller than this one. But at the end of the day, the Bluetti Elite 300 solar generator offers the right balance between a midsize power station that delivers a lot of power and run time, and a station that is compact and portable enough to be perfectly suited for an outdoor adventure.

Full Bluetti Elite 300 Solar Generator Review.

In a recent development, the EcoFlow Delta Pro is a large portable power station with an output that rivals some gas portable generators. When sold in a bundle with solar panels, like the package with two 220-watt portable panels we tested, it becomes a powerful solar generator. With an output of 3,600 watts, the Delta Pro can charge multiple appliances, and the output has the ability to bump up to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if more power is needed.

To get an idea of the run time, we used the Delta Pro to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator—which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes. When recharged from a standard outlet, it took only two hours and 36 minutes. But it also charges with the included adapter, at electric vehicle charging stations, with a DC car adapter, or with the solar panels that come with the unit. Through the 30-amp connection, you can also connect this to a transfer switch to directly power select circuits in your home.

Like any power station with a large battery capacity, it will take a long time, perhaps nearly two days, to recharge this station using the bundled 220-watt solar panels. The good news is the Delta Pro accepts up to 1,600 watts of solar input, so it can charge faster by connecting more panels.

The heavy-duty wheels and telescoping handle on Anker’s Solix F3000 are easy to use, allow you to stand upright when pulling, and are a dream for people who regularly find themselves moving their power station around, whether it’s at a campsite or to different parts of the house during a power outage.

Along with convenience, this generator is a powerhouse with the capacity to easily run your refrigerator or a greenhouse heater, or keep your RV bright and warm.

We were impressed with Anker’s app, which allows us to check the charging status or power being generated without continually going outside to check. The app also lets you turn the power to the AC and USB ports on and off remotely, keeping tabs on how much energy is being utilized.

In a recent development, the Solix F3000 has 11 ports, including two car ports, an RV-specific outlet, four AC ports, three USB-C charging ports, and two USB-A. In sunny conditions and moderate temperatures, it recharges with a 400-watt solar panel in just a few hours and supports up to 2,400 watts of solar input.

One of Jackery’s most recent solar generators is also its most rugged, able to withstand the elements better than most. It achieves this with an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system, which is part of a titanium alloy cooling structure that helps keep water out of the enclosure.

Recent findings suggest that we got a chance to see these features up close and were impressed by them all, as well as a very sturdy enclosure that, thanks to the cooling system design, eliminates any side vents that could allow water to get inside. It feels strong; you could bang this station around without worrying too much about damaging it. The only downside is that this denser construction adds a bit of weight.

According to recent reports, as a power station, it delivers 1,800 watts of output with a battery capacity of 1,536 watt-hours. That’s enough power for a weekend camping trip or for running low-powered small appliances and some lighting during an emergency. As a solar generator, it can handle up to 800 watts of input from a portable panel. We paired it with a Jackery 200-watt panel, and it worked well. Overall, if your off-road adventures often get a little dirty, but you need some extra power, the Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station is a good one to have at your side.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review.

According to recent reports, the latest version of the Goal Zero Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping situations where dust, wind, and potentially wet conditions are always on the table. This 2,000-watt power station is weatherproof with an IPX4 rating and features outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs. Each section is well-lit by an LED light that’s individually turned on or off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a certain period).

There’s a healthy number of outputs on the Yeti 1500, including four 120-volt AC outlets, four (two are high-powered) USB-A ports, and four 12-volt connections. We simulated an emergency blackout and managed to run a cable modem with a WiFi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

To test its solar capabilities, we paired the Yeti 1500 with a Nomad 200-watt portable solar panel and connected it using the high-voltage DC input, which accepts up to 600 watts; however, it also features a low-voltage input that accepts up to 300 watts for smaller panel arrays. Because both inputs can be used simultaneously, you could theoretically pair with two arrays for up to 900 watts, which is a high amount of input for a station of this size.

According to recent reports, of course, no portable panel operates at 100 percent efficiency. Even on a sunny, cloudless day with no shade-causing obstructions, the input readings highlighted anywhere from 125 to 145 watts. After initiating a recharge with only 5 percent capacity left, it would take at least 10.5 hours in those conditions to recharge. That’s actually not bad. An average of about 70 percent efficiency for a portable panel is good.

Full Goal Zero Yeti 1500 Review.

Recent findings suggest that the Anker Solix C2000 power station can deliver the full 2,400 watts of output to the bank of five AC outlets—something similar stations don’t offer. This allows you to power several things at once, like a refrigerator, toaster, router, and chargers, all at the same time.

During our tests, we were able to take full advantage of this, powering a refrigerator (by itself for up to 18 hours), along with some high-powered appliances, like a four-slot toaster and an electric kettle (though not the last two at the same time).

Another interesting ability of the C2000 is that you can fast charge it from AC power up to 1,800 watts, but that recharging rate remains consistent if you’re powering other devices at the same time (we confirmed this with a wattmeter). For example, we ran a 1,400-watt space heater while still recharging at the full 1,800-watt rate. Other power stations offer similar fast charging but will throttle the amount of power coming into the station while powering devices.

For solar recharging, we were a bit disappointed that this station can only accept 800 watts of input; other stations of this size accept more. But when solar was plugged in, it worked well. We connected it to a 200-watt Anker portable panel, and in full sun, we were getting around 125 to 145 watts of input, which is pretty good as these types of panels go. The C2000 is not IPX-rated for any type of weather resistance, however, so we would not recommend leaving this station sitting outside if the weather turns wet.

Full Anker Solix C2000 Power Station Review.

Power stations use watts and watt-hours to express size and capacity. Watts (size) refer to how much power it produces. For example, if you need to run a 900-watt microwave, you’ll need a station that outputs at least that much power (ideally more, since factory specs are never exact).

It has been revealed that meanwhile, watt-hours (capacity) give you an idea of how long devices can be powered continuously, though how much time depends on the amount of power being drawn—watt-hours don’t dictate a set time frame. Higher-powered devices will drain the battery a lot faster than lower-powered ones.

That may seem confusing, but a simple equation gives you an approximate idea of how it works: total watt-hours (of the generator) ÷ watts (of the device) = hours the power station runs.

It has been revealed that for example, if you had a power station with a 2,048-watt-hour capacity and wanted to run a 750-watt space heater consistently at its highest setting, it would probably run for around 2.5 hours, so long as nothing else is plugged in. But for a refrigerator, whose power draw fluctuates between 10 and 300 watts (depending on how often the compressor turns on), you might be able to run it for nearly 24 hours.

Keep in mind that manufacturer specs are taken from perfect conditions; in the real world, you’ll likely see slightly less capacity from your power station. If you’re not sure how much power the different devices in your home draw, sometimes it’s written on a label, or you can use a device like a wattmeter.

It has been revealed that just as a power station has specifications on output size and capacity, solar panels are rated by how many watts they produce for a device after they convert the sun’s rays into electrical current (e.g., 100 watts, 200 watts, etc.). Because real-world conditions are never perfect, it’s not uncommon for panels to only output 50 to 75 percent (or even lower) of their total potential.

Your panels must also be within the acceptable input range of the power station. For example, connecting a 400-watt solar-panel array to a power station that only accepts 110 watts of solar input can cause an overload and damage the station.

While weight and size don’t directly correlate to the technicalities of power banks, they impact the convenience of each model. Many camping and overlanding setups have limited space, so the more compact models likely have a higher appeal as a result.

That said, most units weigh at least 10 pounds, and the weight and size increase rapidly with greater capacities. Before purchasing, consider where you plan to store the power bank and the space in your vehicle or camper where it will live while you’re on the road. If you plan to use this power bank solely as a home backup option, portability will matter less, but consider how much effort it will take to move it around within your home or in your outdoor space.

According to recent reports, I am a low-maintenance camper, and most of my background is in lightweight backcountry travel. That means I prioritize space-saving and ease-of-use, so my go-to power banks have between 250 and 600 watt-hours, and weigh less than 15 pounds.

Industry observers note that this is perfect for a weekend trip, with the on-the-go (car or solar) charging capabilities to put my mind at ease for longer trips. Mostly, I’m charging small items, so one charge lasts a long time. However, plenty of people in the van-life and remote-work world are powering their RVs and vans, and relying on multiple laptop charges. For that, I’d recommend one of the larger units.

Industry observers note that A solar-powered generator charges and runs almost anything that requires power—it just depends on the capacity. These generators can charge power tools in the shop, laptops for remote work, and personal devices like Bluetooth headphones and speakers.

A solar-powered generator with a higher power capacity can even power household appliances in the event of a power outage. And the fact that these are solar-compatible means you aren’t reliant on the electrical grid to recharge them.

Every unit on our list has multiple charging options, including wall (AC outlet), car (12-volt), and solar. Each input method charges your unit at a different speed, and solar also depends on the conditions. AC power is the fastest, followed by 12-volt, and then by solar (though a larger solar array could potentially be faster than 12-volt).

I try to charge up my power banks whenever I can, so I’m never caught off guard trying to leave on a trip with a dying power bank. If this happens (which it has), I’ll charge it in my vehicle’s 12-volt port while I’m driving, though this is often slower than solar or a wall unit.

Solar power is the most sustainable and typically fastest way to power these—just be sure you have enough wattage in the solar panels to make it effective. I recommend keeping the generator stored with at least an 80 percent charge, and unplugging it once it’s fully charged—keeping it plugged in longer than necessary degrades the battery.

Most units will have a simple readout display showing the remaining battery charge, and it’s a good practice not to allow your battery pack to get below 20 percent.

He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it might seem strange, the notion that people have been surprised to find that a David Fincher film, written by Quentin Tarantino and starring Brad Pitt, is “actually good.” But moviegoers had their fair share of reasons to be skeptical of The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth: chief among them, that Tarantino was forcing a mind-melding of the auteurs that could prove disastrously incongruous simply because he didn’t want to blow his long-awaited 10th and final film on a sequel. The 10-film rule is, of course, completely self-imposed, a mandate Tarantino is stubbornly sticking to instead of realizing he can still employ strict curation and quality control without limiting his filmography to a perfect even number. But now that he’s actually, finally, on what will be his last movie (according to his rules), there’s this notion that he’s afraid to pull the trigger—which some believe he all but confirmed when, in 2023, he announced his 10th film would be called The Movie Critic, only to completely retract that a month later.

Two years later, Tarantino sat down as a guest on (what else?) The Church of Tarantino podcast, hosted by two QT superfans, which is actually a pretty fun listen in between all the excessive stanning. So promptly do they bring up QT10 that it’s obvious the director was anxious to set the record straight. Tarantino tells the hosts that TMC started as an exercise in attempting to write a compelling story about “the most boring” profession imaginable. Despite succeeding, he realized he wasn’t excited by it once the film entered pre-production. There was also a version of the story that he adapted into an eight-hour miniseries, until he realized he had no interest in the process of selling and making TV either.

It’s similar to the way he’s talked about what became Cliff Booth, which started as a novel before morphing into an unwieldy feature script until Pitt convinced him to let someone else take a crack at directing it, lest these titular misadventures go to waste. Watching the film last week, my ears perked up when, in the midst of being courted by Cliff, high-powered Hollywood agent Karen Crosby reveals she got her start in the industry as a… movie critic. She reflects back on her time writing about film derisively, describing the profession as one with a low barrier for entry.

In a recent development, karen is instantly one of the most beguiling characters in a movie filled with colorful performances both big and small. Played by Elizabeth Debicki with an icy, over-it resolve, Karen’s nagging fascination with Cliff makes for what one critic aptly described as Tarantino’s best-written romance since Jackie Brown. Despite being the closest thing to a co-lead, you walk away from the film feeling like you haven’t seen nearly enough of her.

Later in the film, Debicki gets a showy, highlight reel-worthy monologue where Karen, instead of extolling the virtues of cinema as a former critic might, recites what’s apparently an infamous credo among her close friends: that film, while entertaining, hardly rises to the level of being true art. (This is much to the delight of one of her clients, A-list TV star Charlie Peters, played by Scott Caan.).

It has been revealed that it was at this point that I was certain we were watching remixed and repurposed scenes from The Movie Critic—and that if Karen Crosby wasn’t the eponymous character, she was at the very least a gender-flipped version. In one of the only times Tarantino talked openly about his erstwhile film, he mentioned it would be “based on a guy who really lived but was never really famous, and he used to write movie reviews for a porno rag.” Meanwhile, the internet ran with the idea that the film would actually be a not-so-thinly-veiled tribute to Pauline Kael. Karen, for what it’s worth, name-drops Kael when describing her past life.

Recent findings suggest that that this is among the best scenes in the otherwise thoroughly enjoyable Further Mis-Adventures only underscores how silly Tarantino’s 10-film imposition is. Look, l I agree with him: as a logline, it hardly sounds exciting enough to be a career finale, but a Tarantino-directed version of the movie probably would’ve been a good time given how much the director clearly enjoys luxuriating in this world. He can write odes to ‘60s and ‘70s cinema in his sleep. But because it would be a retread with no 11th script to follow, it’ll never see the light of day.

In a recent development, or will it? I hate to enable weird science, but The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth doesn’t simply work; it’s one of the best movies of the year. Can another director submit himself to Tarantino’s tone and vision the way Fincher does so gamely here? Would Fincher even want to do that again? Hard to say on both fronts, but if Tarantino is going to keep being precious about his next (last?) directorial outing, the least he could do is let someone else execute his other ideas before they start collecting dust. Even Tarantino’s B-Tier is still a great time at the movies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Industry observers note that note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, promptly empty the contents into a fresh pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

Recent findings suggest that to a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

It has been revealed that scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

#158909. The Rise, Fall, and Future of Makeup Artist-Led Brands

The Rise, Fall, and Future of Makeup Artist-Led Brands

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2276 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When news broke in October that Isamaya Ffrench had severed ties with her namesake beauty brand, fans of the avant-garde makeup artist were saddened but not surprised.
  • Ffrench responded to a customer complaint on Instagram in October by apologizing, adding that she was no longer associated with the brand.
  • Industry observers note that though Isamaya Beauty remains operational, speculation about its future has been rife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When news broke in October that Isamaya Ffrench had severed ties with her namesake beauty brand, fans of the avant-garde makeup artist were saddened but not surprised. For months, there had been growing customer frustration about unfulfilled orders and unresponsive support. Buyers reported severe shipping delays, missing or damaged items, and unanswered refund requests across the brand’s Instagram and review sites like Trustpilot. By July, its social media accounts had stopped creating new posts, while inventory markdowns on its website were as high as 70%.

Ffrench responded to a customer complaint on Instagram in October by apologizing, adding that she was no longer associated with the brand. Shortly after, she thanked her followers on her personal Instagram during what she called “an incredibly difficult and emotional time”. The Isamaya Beauty brand did not respond to a request for comment.

Industry observers note that though Isamaya Beauty remains operational, speculation about its future has been rife. It follows the bankruptcy of fellow makeup artist Pat McGrath’s eponymous label earlier in January. Pat McGrath Labs famously hit a $1 billion valuation in 2018, a mere three years after launch, but struggled to scale and keep pace with modern beauty demands. It exited the Chapter 11 bankruptcy process in April under upcoming majority owner GDA Luma, a Miami-based investment firm. McGrath herself stepped down as CEO and transferred her equity to the holding tech giant while staying on as chief creative officer.

While Ffrench and McGrath remain highly respected creative forces (McGrath is the creative director of cosmetics for La Beauté Louis Vuitton, while Ffrench presently runs the interdisciplinary concept store and gallery Studio Iron), the hurdles faced by their namesake labels highlight the structural friction between avant-garde artistry and commercial scaling. Their trajectories also signal a broader reckoning for makeup artist (MUA) brands, which have become a dominant yet deeply volatile segment of the beauty market, characterized by rapid boom-and-bust cycles.

The late 2010s marked an unprecedented period of rapid industry growth. Social media, viral rolls out, and Sephora shelf space helped drive hype for makeup artist-led brands, several of which subsequently enjoyed massive funding and bloated valuations. Many, however, struggled with post-pandemic relevance and debt. Today, the market has become saturated, and shoppers are increasingly fatigued by frequent drops and buzzwords. Consumer preferences are also evolving, with Gen Z opting for customizable, skin-first routines while millennials desire substantive education beyond surface-level trends.

“On the back of the success of brands like Charlotte Tilbury, which grew and ultimately sold to a strategic buyer, more people became interested in putting in capital behind the next generation [of MUAs],” indicates Ilya Seglin, managing director of consumer, retail and e-commerce at Cascadia Capital, citing Patrick Ta, Makeup by Mario, Danessa Myricks Beauty and Westman Atelier. However, many of these brands have not been acquired. Their founders have spoken publicly about choosing to stay independent and fund long-term growth, but at the same time, beauty strategic investors have pulled back on makeup deals.

Charlotte Tilbury at the opening of her Covent Garden, London flagship in 2025.

As Seglin explains, “Strategics have no idea how to get comfortable with color [cosmetics]”, which is increasingly viewed by investors as a “fashion” category — in other words, a volatile, trend-driven sector that is high risk but high reward. Both fashion and MUA-founded labels share the challenges of maintaining quarterly growth while mitigating trend fatigue and inventory risk. Beauty trend cycles, in particular, have accelerated with the advent of online algorithms and short-form content that create rapid microtrends that can rise, peak, and fade within weeks or months, rather than years. “The perceived risk profile of color brands has increased, so strategics have become more cautious. They don’t know if this is like a fashion brand that’s going to be around for 5-10 years, or whether it’s going to be around for longer. Strategics want to acquire brands that are going to be around forever.”.

Despite the risks, makeup artist brands remain attractive to customers, accounting for roughly 30% of the prestige beauty market in the US, according to Larissa Jensen, senior vice president and global beauty industry advisor at Circana. “Makeup artist brands are the largest brand type within the makeup category. Collectively, they’re growing about 7%, which is outpacing total makeup growth,” she explains. “The units are actually performing, up 5%, compared to makeup overall, which was flat. That’s an indicator of demand.”.

Still, MUAs have come a long way since early pioneers Bobbi Brown (1991), François Nars (1994) and Laura Mercier (1996) disrupted traditional department-store beauty, bringing their backstage and editorial expertise to everyday consumers via wearable neutrals and face base products. The subsequent rise of Instagram and YouTube transformed makeup artists like Charlotte Tilbury into global personalities. By the late 2010s, A-list celebrities and influencers (think Kylie Cosmetics by Kylie Jenner, Fenty Beauty by Rihanna and Rare Beauty by Selena Gomez) flooded the market. Meanwhile, contract manufacturing enabled independent, founder-led brands (like Glossier and Morphe) and beauty vloggers with massive, highly trusting audiences (such as Huda Kattan and Jaclyn Hill) to launch swiftly and market directly to consumers. Built-in audiences and excited VCs temporarily overshadowed traditional artist-founded lines.

Bobbi Brown applying makeup on model backstage at Tory Burch SS07.

As consumers grow weary of celebrity white-label lines, credibility is shifting back to working makeup artists. Mary Phillips (M.ph Beauty) and Mario Dedivanovic (Makeup by Mario), for instance, regularly share behind-the-scenes details, signature techniques and product breakdowns from their red carpet prep with the likes of the Kardashian-Jenners. Both artists have long been part of the family’s glam squad and turned their routines into global beauty trends and brands.

Meanwhile, some modern founders didn’t come from traditional channels like celebrity glam or print magazines, but can demonstrate why their formulas deserve permanent space in one’s bag. Jamie Genevieve, for example, built an online following after working on makeup counters in Scotland. Her beauty brand Vieve celebrates its sixth anniversary this month. Sales have grown from £6.5 million in 2024 to £9.3 million by late 2026. Meanwhile, Jordana Ticia’s eponymous label has become one of the UK’s biggest indie beauty success stories in recent years, marked by a 239% increase in TikTok Shop GMV in 2024 (two years after joining the platform) and a May 2026 launch into Space NK where first-week sales beat forecasts, according to the Manchester-based founder.

Many of these modern MUA brands are actively pushing back against traditional “haul” culture by highlighting durability, multi-season versatility and cost-per-wear. Rather than lean heavily on novelty collaborations or viral packaging, the new generation is more focused on approachable, everyday beauty staples that can become high-repeat categories.

Violette, founded in 2021 by the Parisian makeup artist Violette Serrat, has leaned into French attitudes to beauty: to age with ease and feel comfortable in one’s own skin, and to treat skincare and fragrance like food or wine — something to savor and enjoy. Instead of seeking to mask or fix perceived flaws, Serrat — who has amassed over a million followers collectively across her personal Instagram and YouTube accounts — encourages natural-looking, lived-in looks. Her routines often show her applying products with her fingers rather than complex tools.

Violette is inspired by makeup artist Violette Serrat's love for fine art and French beauty philosophy.

Violette’s go-to market strategy was not to launch in Sephora or an equivalent retailer. Instead, the brand launched in locations like Oh My Cream, a “clean beauty” concept store, and French pharmacies, which in her view offered a real “stamp of approval” given their penchant for products that are simple, consistent and credible. Violette’s top sellers include the Bisou Balm (a lipstick-balm hybrid that creates a soft, blurred look) and Boum Boum Milk (a 3-in-1 skincare spray combining toner, serum and moisturizer).

In a recent development, serrat’s belief is that while brands don’t have to speak to everyone, their products need to be universally understood. “I think it’s ok to be a little bit more niche. But my mission as a makeup artist is to simplify my technique,” explains Serrat, whose makeup has appeared editorially in American and French Vogue, and on the red carpet via figures such as Léa Seydoux and Natalia Vodianova. “If you look at my work, it’s very complex makeup. But for my brand, I want to make sure my products are understood on an instinctual level. You just put your finger in and do it.”.

Industry observers note that the British makeup artist Katie Jane Hughes, who counts a total of over two million followers across TikTok and Instagram, also bridges playful artistry with accessible, skin-first education. Rather than pushing rigid beauty rules or complicated tutorials, Hughes offers practical breakdowns and techniques that let natural skin texture show through. After years of working with high-profile clients such as Emmy Rossum, Kerry Washington, and Dua Lipa, among others, Hughes — who is based in Newly introduced York — founded her beauty brand KJH in 2023, selling a tight lineup of accessibly priced items including the Precision Sculpture Stylo (a sculpting liner for the lips or eyes) and Microscara (a mascara with a petite brush built for better control). Sales have grown 250% year on year.

Core to KJH is its ability to reach a wide demographic of people. A poll conducted independently by KJH found that only 10% of the brand’s customers are makeup artists or fellow creatives. “Most of the people are not professionals. So I wanted to create products that allow them to feel like they’re more of an expert with what’s in their makeup bag,” states Hughes. As of August, the brand has expanded from DTC into Sephora in the US and Canada. Asked whether it’s a pivot in strategy, Hughes explains that cosmetics are deeply sensory products that rely on in-person testing and trust. “I like playing with a product in person before buying it. I think that’s really important.”.

British makeup artist Katie Jane Hughes has won over a loyal audience for her approachable tutorials, signature glowing aesthetic and rule-breaking attitude toward beauty.

Built on technical skill and real-world experience, makeup artist-founded brands continue to stand out from celebrity or creator cash-grab lines. More are also expected to come to market, with the next highly anticipated launch to potentially come from celebrity makeup artist Nina Park, if early trademark filings are any indication. However, as Circana’s Jensen warns, “how many of [those MUA labels] really blow up and become huge or mainstays remains to be seen.”.

Indeed, Violette, which is not yet profitable, raised $5 million from three existing investors in May, extending the Series B round that originally closed in 2024. It’s significantly smaller than the earlier sky-high multiples some MUA labels have previously commanded. Nonetheless, the recent funding indicates investor optimism and wider appetite for Violette, which Serrat is confident can reach profitability in the short term. The brand has entered latest doors, including Sephora in the US as of 2025 and the UK this November. According to Serrat, sales at Sephora have doubled year over year, and the brand has since been “fast-tracked” to roll out in 800 doors, including in Canada, up from 80.

Taking on investment means toeing the line between creativity and commerciality. “If you’re niche, you cannot have investors,” she claims, matter-of-factly. “You can do a super niche and creative brand, but you have to be self-funded. For me, raising money made me anxious. I needed to make sure I was able to have a very healthy business. You can create a brand that is inspiring, but at the same time, you need to think of the bottom line. It’s my obsession. I want to be profitable as soon as I can.”.

It has been revealed that it’s for these reasons KJH is primarily self-funded and has operated without traditional outside venture capital or institutional funding rounds since its launch. Hughes stressed the need to work at her own pace, despite ongoing interest from incubators and VCs alike. “I didn’t want to be tied to anybody. I didn’t want to feel like I had this big organization above me telling me what I should do next,” she explains. “Now, we have more of a steady flow of sales, allowing us to have more launches throughout the year. We’ll probably release two to three products a year versus just one. But it’s because I want to do it. I want to do what’s right for me and my community.”.

Hughes's beauty brand KJH focuses on multi-use formulas and practical makeup education.

It has been revealed that however, experts also say that more than ever, consumers are looking to credible industry leaders and specialized experts to cut through the noise and AI-driven information overload. “For makeup artists, it’s really about bringing forth their expertise. There’s an authenticity that comes with their brands,” says Jensen. “Within the hair category, salon brands are the largest. Within skincare, it’s clinical brands founded by doctors or cosmetic chemists. What that collectively says about the consumer is that they are looking for expertise in their categories.”.

Seglin adds that investor sentiment — like consumer trends — is cyclical. And the current funding constraints may, in fact, be beneficial for both the market and MUAs. “It forces them to actually be good. They will probably be better businesses than the brands that were flooded with investor cash before.” Those eager for a payout need to “be realistic about market dynamics”, he claims. “If your expectation is to raise $10 million to launch a brand and in three years you’re going to sell to L’Oréal, I would temper those aspirations.”.

  • According to recent reports, start the Bolognese sauce: Heat 2 Tbsp.
  • According to recent reports, add the meat: Stir in 1 lb.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’ve always loved Italian American food. Maybe because Italian and Korean cooking have traits in common: Both are homey and resourceful, and grandmothers are revered for their signature dishes made without formal recipes. This recipe was one of the first Korean Italian fusion recipes I developed, and it makes use of my two favorite secret weapons: kimchi and fish sauce. The result is the Bolognese you know and love, but with a deep, tangy twist. Fish sauce in Italian cooking is not a latest idea, actually—Romans have been using salted anchovies and garum, an ancient kind of fish sauce, for centuries. For an extra-special finish, I love garnishing this with baek (white) kimchi for acidity. But it’s optional, and regular kimchi (or no kimchi) works just fine, too.

More winning pasta recipes this way.

According to recent reports, start the Bolognese sauce: Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or pot over medium-high heat. Stir in 1 medium-yellow onion, finely diced (about 1½ cups), 2 carrots, peeled and finely diced, and 3 stalks celery, finely diced, and cook, stirring occasionally, until the onions have softened and the edges start to brown, about 4 minutes. Stir in 4 cloves garlic, minced, and a pinch of kosher salt and cook for 30 seconds, then stir in 1 cup chopped kimchi and 1 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook until the kimchi pieces start to soften, about 3 minutes. Pour in ½ cup red wine, increase the heat, and simmer, stirring with a wooden spoon to dislodge any bits that have stuck to the bottom, until the wine has nearly disappeared, about 2 minutes.

According to recent reports, add the meat: Stir in 1 lb. ground beef, season with generous pinches of salt (at least ½ tsp.), and cook, breaking up the beef into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until cooked through, 6 to 8 minutes.

It has been revealed that add the tomatoes: Pour one 28-oz. can whole San Marzano tomatoes in a bowl. Using clean hands, squish the tomatoes into small pieces. Pour the tomatoes into the pot and add 1 cup beef broth or water, ½ tsp. dried Italian seasoning or dried oregano, a pinch of salt, and a few grinds of freshly ground black pepper. Bring to a simmer and lower the heat to medium-low. Gently cook, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is just thick enough to stand up on a spoon, about 20 minutes. Stir in 2 Tbsp. fish sauce and taste, then add more salt or fish sauce if needed.

Industry observers note that cook the noodles and serve: In a pot of boiling salted water, cook 1 lb. spaghetti according to package instructions, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking, until al dente. Drain the noodles in a colander, then give the colander a shake to get rid of extra water. Divide the noodles among serving plates and spoon the Bolognese on top. Garnish with 1 cup chopped kimchi (white or regular; if using) and 2 Tbsp. chopped flat-leaf parsley and serve.

Do Ahead: Leftover Bolognese sauce (without the noodles) keeps in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days, or in the freezer for up to 2 months.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that whether you're hosting a small gathering this year or simply craving the comforting flavors of Thanksgiving any time of year, this sheet-pan dinner is the way to go. It’s a feast that’s as cozy as it is convenient, bringing together the classics with a few flavorful twists. The beauty of this meal lies in its simplicity—everything roasts together on a single pan, making cleanup a breeze.

Sources indicate that the turkey:Using a bone-in split turkey breast helps ensure juicy, flavorful meat with rich, golden skin, slathered with butter and seasoned with poultry seasoning. This nod to tradition is enhanced with a touch of smoky paprika and garlic to amp up the flavors. For the stuffing, I went the classic route, using store-bought seasoned cubes for a bit of nostalgia, along with onions, celery, and soy sauce to boost the savory notes, and cranberries for a hint of sweetness. The stuffing offers the best of both worlds, with crispy edges and an irresistibly savory center soaked in turkey drippings.

The sweet potatoes:The sweet potatoes strike a perfect balance, spiced with warm and aromatic garam masala—a perfect pairing with the sweet yet earthy tuber. A splash of orange juice adds a tart-sweet touch, while pecans provide a satisfying crunch. If garam masala isn’t your thing, a dash of pumpkin pie spice works beautifully.

The green beans:The green beans, a nod to the iconic casserole, are streamlined for the sheet pan, tossed with mushrooms, Parmesan, and thyme-infused butter, and finished with crispy fried onions for that quintessential touch.

Make-ahead & storage:If the idea of making a whole Thanksgiving dinner on a sheet pan in one day feels daunting, here’s a tip—prep some components ahead of time. Most, if not all, of the ingredient chopping, grating, toasting, etc., can be done 2 to 3 days in advance. The stuffing can be made a day ahead; just be sure to cool it completely before refrigerating. Even the turkey can be buttered and seasoned the day before, leaving you with just the assembly and roasting on the day of.

According to recent reports, as people who write about food and kitchen gadgets for a living, Bon Appétit editors are constantly surrounded by a wide range of products. This month, holiday-ready martini glasses, turmeric-laced bone broth, and digestion-friendly tea.

Read on for all the products we obsessed over in November.

This summer, I spent a week in Paris with my family and gloriously found myself eating steak frites on more than one occasion. Besides the perfectly cooked bavette and thin, crisp fries, I was enamored with the bistro aesthetic—down to the super-sharp and sleek steak knives I used for each meal. When I came across Made In Cookware’s set, I knew it was a sign that I, too, could adopt this sophisticated French look. These knives are manufactured in Thiers, France, a region known for knife-making, which speaks to their aesthetic and craftsmanship. I love that they’re non-serrated; the sharp edges maintain the integrity of meat and can be sharpened once dull. These steak knives are also full tang, which means they’re constructed with a single rod of stainless steel from tip to handle. And speaking of the handle—the feature that attracted me to this set in the first place—they come in several materials, including olive wood, black polymer, and (my pick) pearlescent acetate. — Melissa Knific, contributing editor.

Industry observers note that what is a martini glass if not a tiny birdbath for my olives? These Year and Day glasses are my favorite kind: classic and elevated, but durable. They’re great for anything you’d serve up, and the best part is that I can set them in the dishwasher at the end of the night. —Casey Hendricks, executive director of audience development.

A woman in her late 20s who starts her mornings with a mug of bone broth as the weather gets cold—I know I’m a cliché. But this chicken bone broth from Fond, specifically the turmeric and black pepper variety, truly does start my day off on the right note. There’s eight grams of protein per cup, sure, but my favorite part is that it’s made without alliums (like garlic and onion) so it’s especially kind to my tummy. Instead, the broth gets its flavor from carrots, turmeric root, celery, lemon juice, cracked black pepper, and thyme. All the vegetables Fond uses are organic and they use 100% pasture-raised chicken, so it’s as close to making my own bone broth at home as I can get, without having to simmer a pot for 18 hours. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager.

M6HG Instant Hot Countertop Reverse Osmosis Water Filter.

Sources indicate that there were a couple of things happening at my house at the same time: First, my wife’s lovely and enormous collection of houseplants continued growing; second, we decided to get a water softener to fight against the notoriously hard water in my part of New Jersey. Those two things don’t go together well because softened water and its added sodium can be bad for plants long term. A reverse osmosis system is one way to fight against that, but we didn’t have the budget (or really the need) for a whole-home RO system, nor did we have the space under our sink for one of those. Enter Waterdrop’s countertop RO. The M6HG has an autofilling pitcher that makes plant care convenient, but it’s also turned out it’s getting more use than our fridge filter for drinking. Water comes out a chilly 48 degrees and measures precisely to 4, 8, or 16 ounces (which my kids love for some reason). It also dispenses at 77℉, 113℉ (supposedly good for baby formula), 131℉, 149℉, 167℉, 185℉ (for delicate tea), and 203℉ (for French press or pour-over coffee). Oh yeah, it’s on big sale for Black Friday. — Noah Kaufman, senior reviews editor.

In a recent development, I never grew up with advent calendars, but I can totally see what the fuss is about. My family and I take such joy opening up a window of surprise every morning. Since the advent calendars in our home are usually food-related, we’ll enjoy the treat together later in the evening, with varying degrees of jostling, depending on what it is. Well, looks like the 2026 holiday season will be another one of us throwing elbows because we have our hands on BonBon’s magnificent Lighthouse Advent Calendar. No paper windows here! The cool Swedish confectionary’s calendar is actually a long tower filled with 24 individually wrapped, numbered mini bags of vegan gummies. The daily candy should be a mix of BonBon’s exclusive fresh flavors as well as its beloved classics. I think my Swedish husband and daughter are already losing their minds (it’s only November) and I’m already fearing for our next dental visit, but it is giving this exceptionally fast holiday season a good reason to stop and appreciate a fun, sweet moment every day. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food director.

Industry observers note that ’Tis the season for...soup. My Dutch oven and I have been on a tear making favorites like white chicken chili, chicken-lentil soup, and tons of minestrone. In my attempt to “be frugal,” I’ve been bringing my soups to work for lunch in my, yes, ludicrously capacious bag, and more specifically, my 20 oz. insulated thermos by Hydroflask. It’s truly the perfect size for a lunch-appropriate portion and keeps my soup warm from morning until around 1 p.m. when it’s time to eat between meetings. It’s completely leak-proof which is crucial for a soup commute. And, it’s dishwasher safe, so when I come home after work, I can just throw it in the dishwasher to use all over again the next day. A small investment for a considerably more delightful desk lunch. —June Kim, executive editor.

Limited Edition Peppermint Mocha Barista.

Recent findings suggest that I’m not really a pumpkin spice latte girl, but a peppermint mocha is a seasonal drink I can definitely get behind—so when I heard that Táche, the brand behind my favorite pistachio milk, had come out with a Peppermint Mocha flavor, I was very eager to try it. Sure enough, it was love at first sip. It tastes deeply chocolatey thanks to the addition of Dutch-processed cocoa, and has just enough peppermint flavor to feel festive and balanced without veering into toothpaste territory. I’ve been mixing it with a shot of espresso over ice to make an easy peppermint mocha latte, but to be honest with you, my favorite way to enjoy it is straight up, chilled and poured into a glass. —Alaina Chou, commerce writer.

Recent findings suggest that I’m often hesitant to use pre-made, packaged products when it comes to cooking. One could say I’m a bit of a control freak, but I’m not opposed to a shortcut, especially when it’s after 7 p.m. on a weeknight and I still need to get dinner on the table.

According to recent reports, enter Gymkhana Butter Masala Mild Simmer Sauce. The London-based, two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant recently introduced a line of sauces, marinades, and chutneys inspired by its iconic dishes. I paired the butter masala sauce with cubed paneer that I rapidly broiled, topped everything with fresh cilantro, and served it alongside basmati rice.

Recent findings suggest that the sauce is rich, complex, and packed with flavor, yet all it requires is a quick reheat. Dinner came together in less than 30 minutes and tasted like something I’d order at a restaurant. Needless to say, I’ll be stocking up on a few more jars. —Ali Inglese, executive producer.

Industry observers note that I’ve absolutely been loving this soothing tisane (aka herbal tea!) from La Vie tea. Produced in the French tradition—and primarily sourced directly from French gardens!—these delicate blends are all made from herbs, flowers, and spices as opposed to tea leaves. The digestion-friendly blend I’ve been enjoying is mostly ginger, fennel, and chamomile, with notes of orange and cinnamon—I’ve been parked on the couch with a huge mug of this brew after many a hearty dinner this month. I’m looking forward to dipping into the lavender-scented “Calm” blend ahead of the forthcoming hectic holiday season! —Rebecca Firkser, test kitchen editor.

It has been revealed that I’m a complete nut for ice cream. Regardless of the season, I’m always ready to pop a pint open for dessert (or a mid-day pick-me-up, let’s be honest). And I can say unequivocally that Graeter’s is my favorite ice cream of all time. Even Oprah agrees with me. She named it her favorite too back in 2002. And thanks to the modern miracle that is dry ice, you can have the best ice cream on the planet sent straight to your door. This option is available year-round, allowing you to pick your own flavors in packs of six or twelve pints (get the Coconut Chip if you know what’s good for you). But if you want to get in the holiday spirit, start with the Holiday Pack. It offers an assortment of seasonal flavors as well as the always in-demand, Black Raspberry Chip. Whether you’re treating yourself this year or shopping for that impossible-to-buy-for friend, this small-batch ice cream from the Buckeye State is the way to go. —Carly Westerfield, manager, audience strategy.
