📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that try as we might, there’s just no changing the hearts and minds of some people, even our dearest loved ones, by presenting them with inconvenient truths. I’m talking, of course, about people who prefer coffee from pods. But based on the popularity of coffee pod machines, it seems those of us who haven’t been assimilated into pod people are outnumbered. And, to be fair, even if the quality of their coffee is all over the place, we can’t deny their convenience. My goal here is to find single-serve coffee makers that can blend that convenience with coffee I actually want to drink.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to plastic and aluminum pods, there’s a bevy of grounds-based coffee makers that specialize in one-cup-at-a-time brewing. So if you’re interested in the ease of pod machines, low-volume coffee brewing for one, or just can’t avoid K-cups, here are the machines that brewed the best.

Sources indicate that thanks to the revival of pour-over and French press coffee making and the proliferation of chic matte-finish electric kettles, there are plenty of ways to brew a single cup of coffee without a dedicated machine and, in general, they give you better results. We will also note that many fancier drip coffee makers (like our favorites from Fellow and Oxo) can now be programmed to brew just one cup of coffee at a time—and do so without the plastic waste of pods. If you want true versatility and have the counter space, we’d advise you to consider a machine that will let you brew for yourself or a crowd, if needed. But we understand the convenience factor of capsule machines, which is why, if you must pop a pod for your daily cup, we’ve made our recommendations below, plus suggested some non-pod options too.

In a recent development, updated 11/25/26: Nespresso is phasing out it's old Vertuo Plus machines but never fear, the fresh Vertuo Up is an even better version of the original and it's our new top pick. And in other news, Keurig released its first completely K-Cup-free machine, and the new Alta platform is really quite good. That makes it the first Keurig machine we've ever recommended.

Vertuo Plus Coffee and Espresso Maker by Breville.

Caffeinator Single-Serve Coffee Maker.

Custom Grind & Brew Single Serve Coffee Maker.

Size: 5” x 18" x 10.5”Water reservoir capacity: 47 oz.Colors: 4Coffee sizes: 1.3 oz., 2.7 oz., 5 oz., 8 oz., 12 oz., 18 oz.

Industry observers note that what we love: Everything we loved about the original Nespresso Vertuo machine is present in the Vertuo Up. The centrifugal brewing method patented for Vertuo machines makes more balanced, better extracted coffee than most typical pod and capsule methods that just shower the grounds with water. And Nespresso continues to expand the world of capsules you can use, now featuring a number of single origin pods for those who prefer flavor profiles from different growing regions around the world, as well as flavored pods for folks whose regular Starbucks order is 13 words long.

And the Vertuo system also reads whatever capsule you insert and automatically brews at the proper volume, so it really does have one-button operation.

The rotating water tank is a nice touch because it allows the machine to fit in any configuration of kitchen and it's very easy to refill.

In a recent development, but the biggest upgrade is the addition of what Nespresso calls “Coffee Creation” mode, which is particularly good for iced coffee lovers. The extra button tells the machine to brew a more concentrated, smaller dose of coffee. That means it can melt the ice without diluting the flavor of the drink. It also lets you add a healthy pour of milk to hot coffee with the same results.

It has been revealed that what we'd leave: Nespresso pods tend towards darker, roastier coffees. So if you have a thing for fruitier, more acidic coffee, you may be better off with either something that uses whole beans or Keurig's Alta.

Size: 10.84" W × 11.77" H × 19.0" DWater reservoir capacity: 72 ouncesColors: 3Coffee sizes: 1.5 oz. to 12 oz.

For a brand that’s name is pretty much synonymous with plastic pods, Keurig threw us for a loop in 2026 when it unveiled Alta, its first plastic pod-free system. Alta is still a single-serve machine and it still uses a capsule of sorts, swapping those little cups for AltaRounds, tablets of ground coffee held together by a compostable vegetable-based coating. Each AltaRound is printed with a QR code that tells the machine what drink styles it should offer up on the touchscreen display from said coffee, whether it is a smaller espresso tablet or a larger flavor coffee round.

Sources indicate that what we love: In my experience, this is the first machine with any association to Keurig that I’ve actively enjoyed the coffee from and kept returning to. For contrast, the whole time I tested the Alta, I had my usual DeLonghi machine set up but a few feet away and for weeks I didn’t touch it because the coffee I really liked the coffee I got from the Alta. There were nuances between the different roasts, from light to medium to dark, and detectably different intensities in the espresso rounds. (Keurig’s announcement states that Peet’s coffee is already on board for future AltaRounds offerings and more partnerships are on the way.).

Customization, while usually limited to three dots indicating temperature and brew strength, was also effective, if a bit. When selecting a milk-based drink, the frother did an impressive job of adjusting to various temperatures and thicknesses, though I did find I usually had to scoop a good bit of any super airy cold foam or cappuccino foam from the pitcher with a spoon.

Navigating the menu was clear and easy. And once I got the hang of it, I found many aspects of the Alta, like the generous 72-ounce water tank and easy to empty drip and used coffee trays, or the simple swaps from hot to iced, to be seamless and a pleasure to use.

What we’d leave: First, it’s a large machine at 19 inches deep, occupying significant counter space, and while part of that has to do with the milk frothing apparatus, it’s also because the AltaRounds and separate K-cup slots are side-by-side, meaning if and when the brand just made the leap to an AltaRounds-only machine, it could probably be a good bit smaller. The automatic nature of the frother is handy, but pouring my own milk in a world of automatic dispensers on super-automatic espresso machines, left it up to me to set up the milk and do the pouring which may be more work than most Keurig converted coffee drinkers are used to. The generous water tank I called out above is slightly limiting in terms of where it allows you to set the machine up. It slides in or out from the side and if you don’t have space next to your Alta to do that, this could pose a problem. I also found the pours a bit splashy, and constantly had little droplets of coffee on the machine and on the counter nearby.

Sources indicate that the touchscreen placement is a little wonky. It’s flat on top of the machine making it a little hard to read, and it’s actually housed in the lid for the AltaRounds slot, something that a fresh user (or houseguest) might not realize, as the K-cup slot is more readily discoverable with no screen and a lip for lifting it up. I fully put an AltaRound into the K-cup slot on the first go around before I more carefully read the instructions. This machine connects to WiFi, which is probably important for downloading new coffee brand specs as more AltaRounds become available, but my software updates were sometimes sticky and required unplugging the machine to unfreeze it.

Lastly, just to harp on the elephant plastic pod in the room, the Alta as it stands feels like a bridge machine to something better, but because of the sheer magnitude of the K-cup world Keurig has created, we’re stuck with a hybrid that feels part past and part future.

Caffeinator Single-Serve Coffee Maker.

Size: 12.6"H x 4.5" W x 14" DWater reservoir capacity: 48 oz.Colors: Concrete, MidnightCoffee sizes: 4 oz., 6 oz., 8 oz., 10 oz., 12 oz.

Sources indicate that what we love: If you’re looking for a streamlined, smart-looking machine to brew your K-cups, Chefman’s Caffeinator wraps its pod machine in a chic shell. There’s a snazzy drip tray that slides up and down for differently sized cups, and backlit touch buttons that disappear into the satin finish exterior (in Concrete or Midnight) when not selected. In addition to looking good, it also produced a pretty good cup of coffee, both from pods and grounds thanks to three simultaneous streams of water.

It offers a lot of customization possibilities, with three hot temperature options from “warm” to “piping hot” (the latter of which raised the temp about 20 degrees from default “hot”), plus a lower temp iced coffee mode, and three brew strengths in addition to multiple cup size selections. It's also compatible with both K-cups and ground coffee. All that gave me the ability to get my coffee a little closer to the way I want it, even if it comes from a plastic pod.

In a recent development, what we’d leave: Clearance for larger cups and tumblers is pretty low, unless you remove the drip tray entirely, which gives you 8.25" of height. But doing that leaves a ring and fixed “divot” about the width of a cupholder that some bigger travel mugs still may not fit into. I wish the water tank was a bit bigger, wasn’t rear-mounted, and had a sturdier lid, however it requires only a slight lift to remove it from the base so it’s easy to manage, even if you can’t see behind the machine. I would have also liked a place to store the K-cup/grounds adapter inserts when not using one or the other.

Custom Grind & Brew Single Serve Coffee Maker.

Size: 15.71" H x 7.99" W x 11.47" DWater reservoir capacity: 58 oz.Color: Black Stainless (only one option)Coffee sizes: 8 oz., 10 oz., 12 oz., 16 oz., 20 oz., 24 oz.

In a recent development, what we love: Why settle for stale pods when you can have freshly ground coffee at the touch of a button? This single-serve machine from Cuisinart has a built-in stainless-steel conical burr grinder that grinds beans only when you’re ready for a cup of coffee. The bean hopper holds up to half a pound of coffee beans and has a gasket-sealed lid to keep them relatively fresh (a seemingly simple feature that my fancy grinder-equipped espresso machine lacks).

I was also impressed with the fineness of the sediment that was left in the bottom of my cup using the mesh filter. You should expect anything that uses only a mesh filter to leave at least a little bit of ground coffee sediment, but in this case it wasn’t unappealing during the last sips. If that is the sort of thing that bothers you, the basket is also paper filter compatible. Grinding and brewing are relatively quiet operations that probably won’t wake anyone up, and gentle beeps let you know your coffee is ready. Also, while you’ll need to find a carafe or container that fits under the machine, the fact that the Cuisinart can brew up to 24 oz. of hot coffee means you could, in a pinch, use this for a few guests over for brunch.

In a recent development, what we’d leave: Cleaning the filter after every use is a chore (and some people choose single-serve machines specifically to avoid that chore by using pods) That noted, there are more gentle beeps to remind you the filter access door hasn’t been opened since the last brew, so at least you won’t forget. Clearance for cups, even with the drip tray completely removed, is still rather low for travel cups at just seven inches. Also, when brewing at the 24 oz. setting, the coffee was noticeably weaker than smaller cup sizes.

Size: 11.5" H x 7.5" W x 10.6" D (plus positionable water tank)Water reservoir capacity: 20-plus oz.Colors: Black, Linen (white)Coffee sizes: 5 oz.–20 oz.

Industry observers note that what we love: Portland, Oregon–based Ratio takes its coffee maker design seriously, including its smallest entry, the Ratio Four, so named because it brews a maximum of four 5-oz. cups of coffee in a single batch. The machine couldn’t be simpler; it uses one button that brews however much water is in the reservoir and a filter basket with flat bottom paper filters. Turn it on, and the first of three lights illuminates to let you know it’s in Bloom mode, followed by Brew and Ready when your coffee is done. The Ratio heats brewing water to an average of 200º F and has a wide stainless-steel showerhead that evenly wets the coffee grounds, producing a full 20-oz. brew that was robust, strong, and exactly what I like to wake up to.

Sources indicate that but we’re here to talk about single-serve coffee, and while using it for one cup is a little trickier (you’ll have to measure smaller quantities of water and coffee), the Four delivered the same bold, balanced brew in a 5-oz. cup, it did in a 20-oz. carafe. I found the recommended 9 grams of coffee lacking, but the instructions advise customizing the ratio a bit, and sure enough a few more grams in the filter did the trick. I found I got the tastiest results brewing two cups (10 oz.), as I think the longer siphoning and heating process with more water flowing through the system was key to a more satisfying extraction. Plus, I like a major cup of coffee.

The Ratio Four comes with a handblown 20-oz. glass carafe that also has a sealed lid and a silicone padded bottom. But what I appreciated is the ability to brew directly into any container; there is no hidden button or latch that the carafe needs to activate to brew or let water through. I could use a mug or travel tumbler if I wanted to. And, surprisingly, the same goes for the filter basket, with the Ratio website and instruction booklet explaining that they’d be just fine with you using it with a Kalita Wave or Origami pour-over dripper if you want. A long-press of the brew button also lets you choose between the default (4 oz. of water) bloom and a shorter (2 oz.) bloom, which is preferable if you are brewing a single cup.

Industry observers note that all of the removable parts are hand-wash-only, but I never found them needing more than a rinse between uses. The instructions recommend occasional cleaning and descaling with an approved solution to keep the lines clean, though, which is important maintenance for any coffee maker.

It has an external, detached water tank that takes up more counter space than it would if it were flush with the machine, but that cuts both ways. I actually love that it’s connected via a sturdy yet flexible hose, allowing you to position it on either side of the machine in a variety of ways depending on your specific needs.

Recent findings suggest that what we’d leave: Ratio is a brand known for machines with parts that feel very high quality, as senior editor Noah Kaufman has pointed out in his reviews of its other two machines. Some of the Ratio Four’s parts are definitely in line with that reputation, like the heavy braided hose between the brewer and water tank. But there are exterior parts of the brewer that do feel less substantial than you might expect for something that costs $279. I also found myself double-checking that the filter basket was installed correctly, because it doesn’t click or snap to signal it’s on right.

Industry observers note that “Set it and forget it” coffee drinkers should take note that the water reservoir isn’t “smart,” meaning it will brew whatever water is inside, so a full reservoir with a coffee mug underneath will overflow. If that’s something you don’t want to think about, the Cuisinart Custom Grind and Brew might serve you better as it requires less frequent refills.

Size: 19" x 6" x 16"Water reservoir capacity: 80 oz.Colors: 2Coffee sizes: 2 oz., 10 oz.

What we love: We have an in-depth review of the Cumulus cold-brew machine for more details, but here’s the gist: You could, in some ways, consider this the Nespresso of cold coffee with its recyclable aluminum capsules that are filled an even more concentrated cold-brew concentrate. The machine does the job of chilling water via an onboard compressor, meaning you don’t need ice in your cup. For texture, the Cumulus offers three settings—still, nitro, and espresso—making it one of the best machines we’ve tried for cold coffee connoisseurs. (Oh, and it achieves that “nitro” coffee without any gas canisters by using ambient air.) It vacuums out the capsules, leaving them empty and ready to recycle after you’re done brewing. And at just 6", wide it’s got a relatively small footprint and front-loading water reservoir, making it easy to use and keep on the countertop.

What we’d leave: At its current nearly $700 price tag, this is a luxury item—though, if you’re dropping $5 on cold brew every day, maybe it isn’t?

Sources indicate that with so many brands and varieties of pods out there, I did my best to compare apples to apples by using Starbucks pods and beans of the same roast for every machine (Bruvi being the only exception that doesn’t sell Starbucks pods). That’s not because the global corporate coffee giant is my favorite coffee roaster, but because it is the most cross-pollinated among all types of machines and formats. For Keurig machines, I also tested using K-cups from Illy coffee, which I’ve found produce stronger coffee (an attribute testers often flag as missing from Keurigs). I used fresh grounds for any machines that offered a refillable pod and whole beans of the same roast were used on machines with grinding capabilities. I also tested the different brew size, strength, and style options on any machine with multiple settings.

In a recent development, there are plenty of subpar single-cup coffee makers out there, and life is short, so we don’t think bad coffee needs to be a part of it. We looked for coffee pod machines that delivered balanced flavor and a smooth finish with consistency.

Recent findings suggest that are the pods simple to load and is the interface (buttons or screens) intuitive and simple? Does the water reservoir require constant refill oversight, and is it easy to access? Does the machine require regular cleaning or maintenance to keep working? The ease of use should extend to pod collection and disposal as well. Some machines require emptying the coffee pod chamber after each use. Others collect them for occasional disposal or recycling.

According to recent reports, pod coffee makers don’t need to take up too much space, but they can also be too small, relying on heating and brewing elements that sacrifice on quality. And because most regular coffee drinkers won’t be putting their machine away every day, it should look good on your countertop too.

Pods are a problem. There’s no way around it. No coffee brewing option will be as ecologically sound as simply pouring water over grounds (and then composting those grounds if you can). Yes, technically you can tear apart Keurig pods, empty their spent coffee into your compost bin and the filter into the trash, and then recycle the plastic cup portion. But overall, we can’t get behind any machine that requires plastic pods that aren’t easily recyclable. Machines that operate using a reusable pod were also given some bonus points.

You’d be hard-pressed to find a better looking coffee machine than the Terra Kaffe Demi. It’s stylish, it comes in four colors, and it’s relatively small for something with a built-in grinder at just over 7" wide—however, it’s nearly 16" deep, and you’ll need access to both sides of the machine, plus the reservoir housed on the back. (If you opt for the milk-frothing TK-02 option, it’ll be wider and deeper still.) Aside from brewing great espresso and pretty great coffee, the most impressive aspect of the Terra Kaffe is how quiet it is. Compared to the cacophony my similarly priced grind-and-brew automatic espresso machine makes, the Demi barely produced a sound.

Generally, I liked the espresso results I got from the Terra Kaffee more than I liked the drip coffee. Once I dialed in my preferred drip settings—which you can adjust for any of the machine’s four drink presets after navigating a maze of menus and submenus—I was impressed with the rich flavor and texture of the coffee with no hint of sediment at the bottom of the cup. For what’s essentially a super-automatic espresso machine with no milk frothing, it’s expensive (commitment-phobes can rent it for $40 a month), so it wouldn’t be my first choice to simply fill a mug in the morning. But if you toggle back and forth between coffee and espresso, it’s comparably priced with other super automatic machines, and it offers a sleek and almost silent option.

Sources indicate that this touchscreen pod machine is everything we wish most K-cup machines could be. It offers rich, balanced, and nuanced coffee, plus eight brewing sizes, one-touch presets for low-acid, americano, iced coffee (which brews hot over ice), and cold brew (which uses cooler water), as well as simple customizations to any of these like temperature control and brew strength. And it does all this using its own proprietary pods made with specially treated polypropylene, which will (mostly) break down in a landfill. So other than you need to use its proprietary coffee pods, Bruvi offers all of the convenience of capsules and the fancy-pants settings of high-end coffee makers and good coffee with little downside.

An espresso machine but make it Nespresso. That’s the idea behind the Creatista series from Nespresso, which adds the automatic milk steaming perfected by Breville, bootstraps it on to a Nespresso Vertuo machine, and wraps the whole thing in handsome stainless steel. It’s great for someone looking for a cappuccino hack. Ultimately we picked the Keurig Alta over the Creatista for this genre of machine because it’s a little less expensive and offers a little more versatility in the form of cold foam options.

Vertuo Plus Coffee and Espresso Maker by Breville.

It has been revealed that the Vertuo Plus does everything the Vertuo Up does sans the iced coffee and full carafe brewing features. The substantial knock on it is that it's being phased out to make way for several other Vertuo machines. But it's still available from third party retailers like Williams Sonoma and Amazon right, often for pretty affordable prices.

It has been revealed that the Essenza Mini comes from Nespresso’s Original line, which uses smaller capsules and only brews 1.35-oz. espresso shots or 3.7-oz. Lungo cups of coffee. And it does so using 19 bars of pressure for extraction, as opposed to the VertuoLine’s centrifugal extraction method. It doesn’t make plain old cups of coffee, however, but we’ve included it here as a good option for pod coffee drinkers who prefer espresso drinks and want a simple way to make beverages like cappuccinos and macchiatos.

Recent findings suggest that like its larger Moccamaster brethren, Cup-One has a timeless, old-school design and a single, tactile glowing “on” switch would make it look at home in a truck stop diner or a trendy modern apartment. And speaking of diners, the coffee, even in a 10-oz. default brew, was diner quality (I mean that affectionately), with robust flavor and texture—though that may have had something to do with the fact that I used the recommended four tablespoons of grounds, twice what other machines suggest for eight oz. Considering its higher price tag, it appears to be pretty low-tech. Okay, okay, it’s just an automatic pour-over machine. But it brewed one of the best single cups from grounds I’ve had from any drip machine. And it’s quiet with no bubbling or burping. What can I say? The small footprint and retro vibes also won me over. It’s a small luxury. It’s a vibe. As the kids say, it’s aesthetic.

Industry observers note that now for the minuses: Yes, you could get a (really nice) gooseneck kettle and pour-over system for, like, half the cost. Give and take. Low clearance under the drip spout means you’re stuck with brewing into mugs and low-profile tumblers. The included measuring scoop and a needle-like poking tool for clearing the filter holder have no home onboard the machine, adding to your “things we need to keep but don’t know where else to put” drawer.

According to recent reports, of all the podless machines, this one is the most podlike in its convenience while producing pod-beating coffee. The eponymous Scoop is a small mesh filter that doubles as a measuring spoon. Just scoop up (or in) your grounds to the maximum fill line, and you’re good to go. The Scoop sits in a second “grounds catching” mesh filter which, in my tests, reduced silt in my cup compared to similar single-filter systems, but didn’t eliminate it. Using the two size settings, you can brew either 8 oz. or 14 oz. per cup. The coffee it produced on normal brew mode was fine, but tapping the BOLD setting did actually produce much more robust results. However, each cup I made was on the oily side.

It has been revealed that A flip-down drip tray holds standard mugs, while the lower drip tray has a clearance of 7", so lots of travel tumblers stand a chance. The 40-oz. water reservoir is on the small side, but is easy to access and lift off from either side with a molded-in handle.

Industry observers note that when you’re done, simple empty and rinse The Scoop (filter) and, if necessary, the secondary filter, and you can brew another cup right away. That’s as long as your Scoop filter is dry, anyway. If it’s still damp from the last cup, you’re going to need to scoop into The Scoop, which basically just makes this like any other small filter machine.

4-in-1 Single-Serve Latte, Iced, and Hot Coffee Maker.

When you think of Mr. Coffee, you probably think of a basic, no-frills drip machine sitting on your grandparents’ countertop. And, for the most part, this multifunction machine is still just a small, simple rain-shower-style drip coffee maker designed for one-cup-at-a-time brewing. The reservoir and reusable mesh filter sit under the lid and feature graduated measurements for water levels from 4 oz. up to 16 oz. You can fill the removable filter with grounds using a double-ended measuring scoop that nests on the side of the machine and has guidelines for different sizes and styles of coffee, whether you’re brewing a “shot” for milk-based drinks or a tumbler full of iced coffee. The bonus of this machine is that, while still retaining a small footprint, it also includes a decent self-contained, stainless-steel milk frother cup with presets for hot milk and cold foam that can be used completely independently from the coffee-making portion.

In a recent development, as for taste and texture, everything was like middle-of-the-road drip coffee. However, I found that following the instructions for the weakest iced coffee (one large scoop) actually gave me decent results that weren’t as watered down as other machines on this list. It also comes with a 22-oz. plastic tumbler just for iced coffee—and enough brewing clearance to fit such a large cup—so if you’re someone who flip-flops between iced and hot coffee and aren’t too finicky about dialing in precise strength, it’s a practical option.

System Coffee and Espresso Machine.

Recent findings suggest that if, for whatever reason, you want to brew Nespresso pods but don’t want to actually get a Nespresso machine, the L’or is your choice. It brews Original Nespresso pods along with its own proprietary pods (which are cross-compatible with classic Nespresso machines). L’or’s brewer offers three brewing sizes and extracts coffee from the pod at 19 bars of pressure through two spouts, similar to the way coffee comes out of a semiautomatic espresso machine. This produces a delicious layer of crema that’s as good as Nespresso’s. It was only in a head-to-head matchup that we slightly preferred Nespresso.

According to recent reports, if you like the idea of Nespresso but not the idea of being stuck with one-cup-at-at-time brewing, the Vertuo Next has brew sizes ranging from a single shot of espresso up to 18 oz. of coffee with the proper pods (an optional carafe is available for the biggest brews). This smart machine also has Bluetooth and Wi-Fi connectivity, so you can track your favorite pods and get firmware updates. However, the Next is a smaller machine than the Vertuo Plus, and with that comes a smaller water tank. And like the Vertuo Pop+ below, the closing and locking mechanism is a bit clunkier than we’d like. But for all out versatility, it’s probably your best Nespresso brewing option.

If you’re looking for a K-cup-compatible coffee machine that can do a little more, this is a good option. It comes with a reusable filter capsule that, while a little finicky getting it to work properly, does, indeed, work. It also has a 72-oz. water tank for less-frequent refills, as well as settings for five cup sizes and two brewing temperatures. The biggest boost we’ll give this machine is that it produced superior tasting coffee using K-cups than any Keurig machine we’ve tried.

We like almost all Nespresso machines, but we think the three recommended above are better than the Vertuo Pop+ for a few reasons. On the Pop+, the actual snapping down of the lid to puncture the pod inside was the clunkiest of the bunch and a lot of effort in a pre-coffee morning fog. And this low-profile machine was so low to the counter, we couldn’t fit a pint glass or similarly sized tumbler underneath, which was a problem considering that Nespresso offers Iced Leggero pods that brew 7.7 oz., overflowing our smaller ice-filled cups. Lastly, the water reservoir on the standard version of this machine (which comes in at 25.4 oz. or 32 oz. on the Deluxe model) is pretty small compared to the Vertuo Plus, and it’s set in a fixed side-mounted position, so you’re stuck with the orientation as is. In other words, it’s still a solid Nespresso coffee brewer but less versatile than what you get for a few dollars more.

It has been revealed that you might consider this machine Lavazza’s attempt to answer the classic Nespresso; its plastic coffee pods and presets brew in espresso or lungo sizes. It beats the Keurig and K-cup machines when it comes to robust and flavorful coffee, but it didn’t live up to the high bar set by Nespresso. The Ristretto capsules we tried were a bit bitter and the texture was thin, though we actually liked the medium-roast decaf capsules enough as after dinner/dessert coffee. Considering Lavazza makes capsules for both Nespresso classic machines and K-cup machines, along with other espresso products, we just don’t think it’s necessary to buy into the Lavazza tech—as sleek and compact as it is—to enjoy its coffee.

Sources indicate that the dual on this machine refers to both drip coffee and coffee pods. It offers multiple brew sizes and strengths, and, being a drip machine first, comes with a glass carafe. It accepts pods with an adapter that fits into the filter basket. Some of its handier features are an adjustable 60-oz. water reservoir, dedicated hot water dispenser, fold-away milk frother, and an adjustable drip tray that allows you to brew directly into a cup or tumbler. But we don’t think it’s the best drip coffee maker out there, and it’s too big and complex for just making capsule coffee.

According to recent reports, there’s a lot to like about the exterior design of this slimmed down version a Ninja single-serve system, from its pleasing colorways like stone, sage green, and glacier blue (in addition to black), its handy fold-away frothing wand that easily whipped some pre-warmed milk into a mug full of foam, or its storage nooks for the pod/grounds adapters and measuring spoon. The generous water tank, while rear-mounted, has a pressure fit lid that actually stays put between the faucet and counter. And all of its detachable parts and pieces are dishwasher-safe. But whether you’ll crave the actual coffee from this machine is another story. Pods tasted weak, even at the lower 6-oz. brewing size, and grounds were better but not by very much. The Specialty Brew setting, which brews a 4-oz. shot of coffee for use with the frother, isn’t quite an espresso experience, either. And while you can choose multiple cup sizes, you can’t select anything but the preset temperature.

Despite its 4.4 stars from over 100,000 ratings on Amazon, we can’t imagine using this machine for coffee every day. Our experience with Keurig coffee pods, regardless of the brand of coffee we tried, was watery or bitter coffee (or, at worst, somehow both). That, plus the fact that this machine’s reservoir is only large enough for one cup at a time makes this one tedious for regular use.

In a recent development, unfortunately, the “smart” features of this machine add more frustration than anything. The machine is supposed to recognize which K-cup you put inside and adjust its brew settings accordingly. It also allows you to select and save brew sizes and temperatures as presets. But in our tests, the machine frequently froze and had to be unplugged to get it going again. Being “smart,” this machine also offers app-enabled remote brewing, something we can’t imagine using since you have to put K-cups in (and take used cups out) one at a time. One plus was the generous 66-oz. water reservoir with a convenient pitcher handle. But in the end, this fancy Keurig didn’t improve our pod coffee experience whatsoever.

As iced coffee rivals hot coffee consumption these days, it’s no wonder Keurig would offer a machine that specializes in cold drinks. One aspect of this machine that’s well thought-out is its dispensing spout, which is high enough off the counter to accommodate a pint glass or tumbler. We found the iced coffee setting only reduced the brew temperature by less than 10°, so our ice still had to do most of the work while also watering the coffee down, which was already diluted with 12 oz. of water during brewing. Even on the smallest of three preprogramed hot coffee brew sizes, it mirrored our other Keurig experiences with weak or just not tasty coffee output.

Oxo 8-cup Coffee Maker with Podless Single Serve Function.

Even though this is an 8-cup coffee maker, I tested this machine because it proudly advertises on the box that it’s also a single-serve machine. Let me get one thing out of the way immediately: This is a great little drip coffee maker if you’re brewing by the carafe. It has the option to brew full and half carafes, and a heated warming plate that keeps the coffee pleasantly hot for hours. But it fell short on a few functional aspects, as well as that single-serve option. First, the water tank is not “smart”—as in, it uses all the water you put in it every time. So if you want a full carafe, you fill it all the way up with water, and if you want a single cup, you put in just enough for… two cups. No, it doesn’t actually brew a single serving of coffee. For a $200-plus machine purporting to do single-serve brewing that can go toe-to-toe with Keurig, that’s a little disappointing.

Additional testing and reporting by Emily Farris.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the crackle of a fire on a cold winter night can add charm to any home. However, fireplaces aren’t particularly efficient heat sources, especially in chilly temperatures. And electric fireplaces, space heaters, and other supplementary heat sources can leave you in the dark (and out in the cold) during a power outage.

Instead, consider adding a wood stove—an appliance that provides a country aesthetic and serves as a primary or secondary heat source. Modern wood stoves can be safe, affordable, and efficient if you clean and maintain them regularly.

Recent findings suggest that more than 2 million of the roughly 12.5 million wood stoves in the U.S. are older, uncertified models that put out far more particulate pollution than newer ones, according to the EPA, and some states prohibit or restrict these wood-burning devices. All of the wood stoves recommended here are EPA-certified, and they still crank out enough BTUs to make your home or cabin cozy.

Before you buy, think carefully about where you’ll install your stove. You’ll need proper clearance from combustible materials in walls and floors, and the stove’s weight has to work for your house.

The Expert (Alex Rennie): I'm a freelance writer who specializes in the Home Improvement, DIY, and Tool space. As a former residential and commercial carpenter, I use my hands-on experience to write practical buying guides, how-to articles, and product reviews. Based in Los Angeles, I spend my free time exploring the beaches and mountains with my fiancé and our dog Louie.

Recent findings suggest that to choose my wood stove recommendations, I selected non-catalytic models that are affordable while still meeting EPA emissions standards. Among the wood stoves that made the cut, you’ll find a wide variety to meet your space limitations and style preferences while maintaining efficient BTU output.

Industry observers note that one of the best things about having a huge fire in the middle of your home is that it lets you make the most of those rustic vibes. Many of the stoves I picked have a cooktop (very convenient) or a large window, so you can put your feet up and enjoy watching the flames. I also relied on prior research conducted by writer Alex Rennie, who also contributed to this article.

In a recent development, this pedestal stove from Ashley Hearth hits the sweet spot between size, heat output, and price. Its 2,500-square-foot heating range fits the average home with room to spare, and the brick-lined, 2.7-cubic-foot firebox accepts logs up to 21 inches long. That means fewer trips to the woodpile on cold nights.

One of the best features is the cast iron door with air-washed ceramic glass, which helps keep soot off the window so you can enjoy the view of the fire. A non-catalytic secondary burn extracts more heat from every load and keeps emissions within EPA standards. It’s mobile-home approved when paired with the optional fresh air kit. The stove runs fine without electricity, but an optional blower will help push warm air into the rest of your house.

According to recent reports, if you don’t need to heat your entire home, this compact Ashley Hearth model delivers plenty of warmth for the money. Its 68,000 BTU output covers up to 1,200 square feet. That makes it a smart fit for a cabin or an open living area, or as a supplemental heat source that takes some pressure off your furnace.

It shares many features with our Best Overall pick, including a firebrick-lined firebox and a non-catalytic secondary burn that keeps emissions within EPA standards. It also has a heavy cast iron door with air-washed ceramic glass. It ships with both legs and a pedestal, so you can choose the look that suits your space. At 258 pounds, it’s relatively easy to move into place, and it’s mobile-home approved with the optional fresh air kit. The trade-off is a smaller 1.3-cubic-foot firebox, so you’ll load logs more often than with a larger stove.

If watching the fire matters more to you than heating every corner of the house, this Superior stove is built around the view. A large rectangular ceramic-glass door gives you a wide view of the flames, and the built-in air-wash system sweeps air across the glass to keep soot off.

It has been revealed that the high-density firebrick holds heat longer for a more efficient burn. It puts out just 2.1 grams of particulate per hour, well under EPA limits. It fits logs up to 18 inches long, and one control handles the airflow. A black pedestal base comes standard, and an optional variable-speed blower can push warm air into nearby rooms.

The trade-off is a heating range of up to 1,400 square feet, so it’s best suited to a living room, a cabin, or a smaller home.

It has been revealed that the WoodPro 300 is the largest model in the WoodPro line, built for anyone heating a large open floor plan, a farmhouse, or a drafty workshop. Its 2.26-cubic-foot firebox takes 18-inch logs and can burn for up to 12 hours on a single load, so you won’t have to refill it every couple of hours.

The stove is made of heavy-gauge steel with a cast-iron door. The Smart Air Control uses two levers, so the lighting procedure is simple: get the fire going, set the air, and leave it alone. It meets EPA 2020 standards at 1.6 grams of smoke per hour with 74.2 percent efficiency, and it’s approved for mobile homes with the outside air kit. Its peak output of 61,700 BTU is modest for a stove rated for 3,000 square feet, so treat that number as a best case in a well-insulated home, not something to count on in a cold climate.

This rustic model from Ashley Hearth—under the US Stove Company umbrella—the US1269E, is a natural fit for log cabin homes that want a rugged addition to their living space, or for anyone looking to add woodsy charm to their home.

My favorite feature is the oversized safety handle, which is comfortable to grab when opening or closing the door and stays cool to the touch, even when the stove is in operation.

It has been revealed that tested and certified to U.L.1482 by Warnock Hersey International, this stove’s 900-square-foot heating range isn’t the largest of my selections, but it's still impressive for its size. The integrated cooking surface on top is also a valuable feature.

It has been revealed that if you’re looking for a pint-sized stove for a small space, including a mobile home, US Stove's Tiny Wood Stove may provide the perfect fit. The slim profile doesn’t mean it’s short on efficiency or on meeting emissions standards, and it still qualifies for the 30-percent Biomass federal tax credit.

Sources indicate that A compact design, however, comes with a few caveats, including a rather small log size and a relatively low BTU output. Still, the US Stove Tiny Stove is a great trade-off for a single-room cabin or a more compact space in your home.

Wood stoves come in all shapes, sizes, and designs. Choose one that suits your space in terms of style and efficiency. Here’s how to decide what you need in a wood stove and what you don't.

In a recent development, there are two types of modern wood stoves: catalytic and non-catalytic. Both reduce air pollution by reburning exhaust to limit emissions, but catalytic stoves use a different process that is slightly more efficient at this second burn. Non-catalytic stoves are popular because they’re less expensive and slightly more efficient at producing heat.

Because the cost of a wood stove with a catalytic converter is right now prohibitive for the average homeowner, the wood stove models we’ve recommended below are all non-catalytic.

More Hot Stuff: Smokeless Fire Pits • Fire Pit Tables • Portable Fire Pits • Heated Blankets.

In a recent development, the size of your wood stove matters not just for the space it can heat, but also for safety. Before you install a wood stove, check your state requirements for clearance. Federal guidelines stipulate that the stove should be installed at least 3 feet from any combustibles in the wall, ceiling, or floors.

If you have children, also consider how much clearance you might need around the stove for a child safety gate and where you plan to stack and store firewood.

According to recent reports, british Thermal Units (BTUs) might sound fancy, but it's just a measurement of how much heat is being generated. This differs from the heating area of a wood stove because it refers to the energy the stove produces in an hour. A rule of thumb: You need 20 BTUs for every foot of space you want to heat. Use this online BTU calculator to dial in exactly how many thermal units your home needs.

Decide whether you’re using your wood stove as a main heating source or for supplemental heat in the winter. In general, a small wood stove can heat about 500 square feet, while a medium wood stove warms up to 1,000 square feet. A large model will heat a room of 1,500 square feet or more.

According to recent reports, more isn’t always better. To keep costs in check and your wood stove efficient, consider if you really need to heat every space in your home or just the living areas your family frequents.

According to recent reports, modern wood stoves are lighter than ever, but many large models can still tip the scales at several hundred pounds. Depending on the stove's weight, you may not be able to install it in a mobile home or in certain structurally vulnerable spots in your house. Instead, look for a wood stove approved for mobile homes by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD).

If your goal is an outdoor wood stove portable enough for camping or backpacking, choose a lightweight model with components that collapse into a compact package.

The size of the logs and the kind of wood you put into your wood stove is about more than convenience or cost. It can also affect burn time and efficiency, which is especially key if you’re using your wood stove as a main heating source.

Sources indicate that generally, most wood stoves fit logs about 16 inches long and 3 inches in diameter. As you can imagine, wood stoves designed for smaller logs may leave you rolling up your sleeves and grabbing the axe more often than you might like.

Since 2020, nearly all latest wood stoves sold in the United States must be certified by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to meet its 2020 emissions standards, which limit fine particle pollution to 2.0 grams per hour (2.5 g/h when tested with cordwood). All of the wood stoves we’ve recommended below meet this standard, and you can look up any model in the EPA’s database of certified wood-burning heaters.

In a recent development, A wood stove’s effectiveness in converting wood into heat is expressed as a percentage of combustion efficiency. Efficiency matters because it directly translates into how much wood you’ll burn to keep your home warm. Most modern EPA-certified stoves fall between 70 and 80 percent efficiency, and every few points add up over a full heating season in fewer logs split, stacked, and hauled inside.

From insulating the chimney to adhering to proper stovepipe clearance, to wall shields and floor pads, there’s quite a bit to do when you install a wood stove, and much of it is mandated by building codes and state or federal laws. To protect your safety, it's critical that you don't miss a step, which is why I recommend leaving the installation of the wood stove to a professional.

Clean your wood stove (and chimney) thoroughly and often to avoid creosote buildup, a highly flammable byproduct of burning wood.

While cleaning your chimney, tidying up your wood stove is pretty straightforward. When the stove is cool, lay down a cloth or newspaper, then empty the ashtray and any ashes from the firebox into an ash bucket. Then wait at least 24 to 48 hours before you dump the ash bucket so any slightly warm embers don’t catch fire.

You can wipe down the interior with a soft, wet cloth and use a chimney brush to scrub out the stovepipe and loosen any residue. If the exterior has rust, you can use a wire brush or sandpaper to remove it.

Sources indicate that yes, you can leave a wood stove unattended for a few hours or overnight, but with some caveats. You should tamp down or mostly close some vents to ensure the fire stays under control. Also, shut and lock the door, and clear any objects from around the stove.

Just be aware that if you blueprint to leave the fire unattended and it goes out overnight, you’ll have to restart it, which is harder than simply feeding a live fire.

Most newly introduced wood stoves you can buy in the U.S. will be EPA-certified, but you should still check the packaging to verify.

EPA certification means the wood stove has been independently tested to meet a particulate emissions limit of no more than 4.5 grams per hour. If you have an old model that is not EPA-certified, check whether your state has a program that provides tax deductions for replacing your wood stove.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A significant, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

In a recent development, welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling).

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Industry observers note that make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too rapidly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Recent findings suggest that do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Sources indicate that just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Sources indicate that spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

Whatever you do, don't let this stock go to waste.

Sources indicate that add all of the ingredients to a large stockpot. Cover turkey completely with water, about 10 to 12 cups.

It has been revealed that over medium heat, bring the stockpot to a boil, then reduce heat and let it simmer for 3 hours. Spoon fat off the top as it rises.

Use tongs to remove the turkey carcass.

Strain stock through a fine mesh strainer. Let the stock cool to room temperature.

Store in refrigerator until ready to use for up to 2 weeks or in the freezer for 3 months.

Stock is the perfect thing to store in your freezer! After letting your stock cool to room temp you can store in the refrigerator for 2 weeks or in the freezer for up to 3 months. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that mcDonald’s has been paying close attention to its chicken menu lately.
  • Sources indicate that mcDonald’s is reportedly testing five hand-breaded chicken menu items in select U.S.
  • In a recent development, the biggest difference with this potential menu overhaul is how the chicken would be prepared.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that mcDonald’s has been paying close attention to its chicken menu lately. Between the return of the Snack Wrap, the introduction of McCrispy Strips, and several upcoming dipping sauces, it’s clear the chain is looking to become a bigger player in the fast-food chicken game. If the latest reports are true, some of its biggest changes might still be ahead.

Sources indicate that mcDonald’s is reportedly testing five hand-breaded chicken menu items in select U.S. markets, including Baton Rouge, Louisiana, and the Tucson, Arizona, area. The information comes from McFranchisee, an account on X that regularly shares details about the chain’s operations and upcoming menu changes.

In a recent development, the biggest difference with this potential menu overhaul is how the chicken would be prepared. Rather than simply introducing latest flavors or sauces, McDonald’s is reportedly experimenting with having employees bread the chicken by hand inside its restaurants.

In a recent development, among the alleged test items is a new McSpicy chicken sandwich. According to the report, all five items are also available as meals, with prices ranging from $8.19 to $9.99 at the location pictured in the social media post.

A similar test is also taking place in Ireland.

In a recent development, I’m particularly interested in how hand-breading could change the texture of McDonald’s chicken. Having taste-tested plenty of fast-food chicken sandwiches and tenders, I’ve found that the breading can make or break the entire experience. A crispier, more substantial coating could make McDonald’s a much stronger competitor to chains like Popeyes and Chick-fil-A.

Rolling out hand-breaded chicken across thousands of restaurants, however, is easier said than done.

The reported tests are designed to evaluate customer demand, preparation costs, and how the additional steps could affect kitchen operations. Some franchisees have reportedly expressed concerns about increased labor requirements and potential kitchen renovations.

While McDonald’s hasn’t officially confirmed the five-item lineup or specific U.S. test locations, the idea of hand-breaded chicken isn’t entirely out of left field.

According to recent reports, during its November earnings call, the tech giant confirmed that it had begun setting up operational pilots for hand-breaded chicken in the U.S. and Ireland. It also announced intends for larger U.S. sales tests at roughly 100 restaurants in early 2027.

Recent findings suggest that for now, there’s no confirmed nationwide U.S. release date or guarantee that all five reported items will make it onto the permanent menu.

Mammut Children's Chair and Table.

Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

📅 01 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1001 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the one thing that can make classic apple pie better?
  • Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers.
  • 2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so initiative ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling).

Recent findings suggest that whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

It has been revealed that make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

In a recent development, place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

According to recent reports, add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

In a recent development, unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

It has been revealed that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

In a recent development, place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

It has been revealed that do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.
