📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

The intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Industry observers note that stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

According to recent reports, do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This dish is built for those nights when it’s chilly outside, and you want something that tastes like it’s been simmering for hours but actually comes together extremely easily. It's a simple one-pan dinner, but the sauce is the star. It’s a mix of tangy balsamic, sharp Dijon mustard, and hot honey. The hot honey adds a glossy, spicy sweetness that makes this perfect for colder weather and coats every bite of the tender, juicy chicken perfectly.

It has been revealed that cooking the chicken:The real secret to this dish is all in the sear. We’re starting the chicken skin-side down to fully render out the fat. This step is crucial as it keeps the skin from being chewy and lets all that rendered chicken fat melt into the sauce, giving it a nice boost of savory flavor. Serve it with white rice or a fluffy rice pilaf to soak up every drop of that sauce. Tip: If you don't have a bottle of hot honey on hand, regular honey plus a teaspoon of your favorite hot sauce is a great backup.

Make ahead & storage:To make ahead, you can whisk the sauce ingredients 2 days ahead and keep it in a jar in the fridge. When you're ready to cook, just sear the chicken and pour it in. For storage, you can keep leftovers in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days.

#158854. Santiago Lastra Wants You to Stop Overthinking Mexican Food

Santiago Lastra Wants You to Stop Overthinking Mexican Food

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1173 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that santiago Lastra might have become a mathematician if it weren’t for a box of Ritz crackers.
  • Then, at 15, Lastra spotted a crab dip recipe on the back of a cracker box.
  • The chef has spent the past month touring the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that santiago Lastra might have become a mathematician if it weren’t for a box of Ritz crackers. Growing up in Cuernavaca, Mexico, the future chef behind London restaurants KOL and Fonda was the sort of kid with more of an appetite for national math competitions. “There would be four questions and five hours to answer those four questions,” he remembers. “I loved that. I wanted to do that for the rest of my life.”.

Then, at 15, Lastra spotted a crab dip recipe on the back of a cracker box. He made it for his family and watched as an ordinary day changed shape around something he had cooked. “I became obsessed with the idea that you can create a special occasion just by cooking something for someone,” he notes. The mathematical brain moved into the kitchen. In his first cookbook, Mexican Soul: A Newly introduced Style of Cooking, Lastra writes about the magic of both disciplines: starting with a few ingredients (or figures) and a recipe (or equation) and creating something greater than the sum of its parts.

The chef has spent the past month touring the U.S. in support of the book: He’s made tacos at Newly introduced York’s Santo Taco, cooked at Yucatan-style seafood spot Holbox in Los Angeles, and enlisted The Bear’s Will Poulter to put a Mexican spin on the Italian beef sandwich at Chicago’s storied Mr. Beef (the real-life inspiration for the show’s original restaurant). Along the way, he’s helped introduce American audiences to a philosophy of Mexican cooking that is as resourceful and intuitive as it is traditional and communal.

It’s an instinct that has taken Lastra on a circuitous journey back home. He started out cooking Italian food, then left Mexico for kitchens in Spain. Various fascinations with French techniques, the experimentalism of Mugaritz, and Upcoming Nordic cuisine followed. “As a young kid, when you leave Mexico, you feel that you made it,” he says. “It took me a long time to realize that what we had in Mexico was really the answer.” Lastra began applying Mexican techniques to local ingredients in Scandinavia, then traveled and cooked across 27 countries. Returning to Mexico to work on Noma’s Tulum pop-up allowed him to look at his homeland with newly curious eyes. “Being Mexican became my superpower,” he says. “I was able to share culture through food, and it opened the doors to the world for me.”.

According to recent reports, KOL was his attempt to make that realization tangible: the Marylebone restaurant that Lastra opened in 2020 cooks Mexican food through seasonal British ingredients. Fonda, its more casual and rambunctious sibling, followed four years later. “I wanted KOL to be one of the best restaurants in the world,” he says, to prove “that Mexican food should be recognized at the level of all the best cuisines in the world.” Not everyone Lastra hoped to touch could ever make it to his London spots or the global pop-ups. “What really makes a difference culturally is the food that people do at home,” he says. “Home cooking is more personal.”.

Mexican Soul posed some questions. How do you cook food that feels fundamentally Mexican without fresh masa, the right dried chillies, or a specialist grocer? Lastra didn’t want readers buying a two-pound bag of chipotle for one dinner. “I had to change the way I think,” he claims. He began writing upcoming rules for the weeknight home cook, rather than an ingredients-led chef. The transition required its own education. He pored over British supermarket aisles, and during a family beach vacation, Lastra locked himself inside to watch hours of Jamie Oliver. He and his brother Eduardo, his collaborator on the book and at KOL, went into a supermarket and decreed that nothing for the shoot could be ordered elsewhere.

Sources indicate that “It tasted great,” he recalls. “I was like, wow… I think I’ve been overcomplicating myself all my life.” Just like in his childhood math competitions, limitations could provide the route to a more interesting solution. The book’s first half teaches some culinary grammar: Sourness, heat, sweetness, smoke, fat, and masa are defined and built into pillar dishes such as guacamole and quesadillas to demonstrate how those sensations work together. “Every time I create a dish, I always see flavors,” Lastra explains. “They’re like your paintings, your colors.”.

The second half gets freer: tomato and cherry aguachile, potato rajas tamales, asparagus pipián. Innovating beyond traditional Mexican cooking, this style is rooted in the cuisine’s history and designed to work with seasonal, local, and accessible ingredients from wherever its cook lives. Lastra resists the idea of Mexican food as something stuck in amber. “The most beautiful thing about Mexican cooking, or Mexican food and Mexican culture in general, is that it keeps evolving,” he states. His proudest—and most last-minute addition—was a tortilla. Nearly defeated by the challenge of creating one without corn masa, Lastra had the novel idea of using mashed potato. Combining it with potato starch, he pressed and cooked the dough, and after days of tweaking, “suddenly it worked and it puffed!” It made it into the book just before printing.

In a recent development, home-testing in the Lastra household has been even sweeter. After we speak, Lastra’s mother—who almost never cooks—is making the book’s mackerel a la Veracruzana for her sons. She’s already sending photographs as she shops for ingredients. “I think she’s never cooked a specific recipe from a cookbook in her life,” he indicates. “So that’s going to be such a highlight.”.

Below, Santiago Lastra’s recipe for albóndigas and Mexican rice, two ways.

Industry observers note that meatballs came to Mexico from the Middle East during the colonial period. They’re a classic of central Mexican home cooking, and are also served in casual eateries called fondas, where they are served with rice and bread or tortillas. The sauces they are served with vary from loose sauces made with cooked green tomatillos to rich tomato and guajillo chilli-based broths. I serve mine in a tomato caldillo with Mexican rice—a classic from our hometown. This is one of my favorite Mexican dishes, and one I would often choose to make if I am hosting friends for dinner.

Sources indicate that red rice is present at most lunches for any Mexican growing up, whether at home or eaten in a fonda. The preparation is simple: rice with peas and carrots, cooked in a tomato and chilli caldillo. The result is a spicy, umami rice with a beautiful color. Serve with stews and tortillas.

Industry observers note that like the red version, this preparation adds a bit of spice, texture, and umami to plain rice. It’s served with all sorts of stews and other dishes in central Mexico, and also with broths like chicken consomé—the kind your mom might make for you when you’re unwell. Fresh jalapeños add a beautiful spicy finish. Perfect with chicken or any other proteins and refried beans.

Mexican Soul, Santiago Lastra (Quadrille) is out now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

A 1991 tuna salad snack started it all, and yes, there's a fan club.

Industry observers note that it’s the morning after Thanksgiving. The good dishes are still drying, the fridge is a Tetris board of foil-wrapped leftovers and you’re standing over the kitchen sink eating cold stuffing with your bare hands. No plate, no judgment.

As it turns out, there’s an entire holiday dedicated to this very specific dining experience. It’s called Sinkie Day, and it’s been around since long before TikTok made girl dinner a thing.

According to recent reports, for that, we have Norm Hankoff to thank. An advertising consultant from California, he had his lightbulb moment in 1991 “while wolfing down some tuna salad over his sink, using extra-strength potato chips as utensils,” according to a 1997 Associated Press report.

Convinced he couldn’t be the only one, Hankoff founded the International Association of People Who Dine Over the Kitchen Sink and declared the day after Thanksgiving Sinkie Day. By 1997, more than 1,000 people had joined, and each one received a membership certificate stamped with a double sink and the group’s motto: “Everybody does it. Sinkies proudly admit it.”.

Sources indicate that naturally, there was a cookbook—or rather, a don’t-cook book. Published by a organization cheekily called Digester’s Reader, The Official Sinkies Don’t Cook Book included such culinary masterpieces as “cakeless frosting” and “meat loaf in your fist.” Other recipes called for little more than a handful of mashed potatoes or a piece of chocolate cake dunked in a glass of milk.

Hankoff even set his sights on 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. When Hillary Clinton was looking for a chef in 1994, he sent her a copy of his book and suggested the first family give sink-side snacking a try. No word on whether they took his advice, but the White House did send him a thank-you letter.

According to recent reports, the beauty of Sinkie Day, which falls on Friday, Nov. 27, this year, is that it’s perhaps the only food holiday that actively encourages you to do less. A fridge full of Thanksgiving extras is all it takes, though a few upgrades never hurt:.

Of course, a holiday devoted to leftovers is also a good excuse to brush up on food safety. As long as everything hit the fridge within two hours of cooking, you’ve got three to four days to work your way through it.

In a recent development, are you a proud Sinkie? Let us know in the comments below!

Gravy-Braised Turkey

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (572 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that cooking a whole turkey is a commitment.
  • In a recent development, this recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now.
  • For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

In a recent development, this recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

In a recent development, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.).

In a recent development, add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

It has been revealed that nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.).

Tech Report: We’ve Been Using Our Gravy Boats Wrong for Decades—Here’s How You’re Supposed to Use Them

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • That little spout on your gravy boat may not be what you think it is.
  • I have a particular weakness for antique dishes.
  • Then I came across an Instagram reel from Steven Moore that made me question something I’ve been doing my entire life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

That little spout on your gravy boat may not be what you think it is.

I have a particular weakness for antique dishes. Most weekends I can be found happily perusing the shelves at thrift and antique stores, where an occasional beautiful piece makes up for an awful lot of cracked mugs and mismatched dinnerware. The gravy boat I use every Thanksgiving was one of those finds. I love it—even though I’ve never been particularly fond of pouring from it. Gravy has an unfortunate tendency to run down the spout rather than into the intended destination—a minor inconvenience of an otherwise lovely piece.

Then I came across an Instagram reel from Steven Moore that made me question something I’ve been doing my entire life. Moore, a British antiques expert, explains that what most of us recognize as a pouring spout on a gravy boat may actually have been intended as a place to rest a small ladle. Excuse me? I’d spent years admiring and collecting old dishware, and somehow this particular bit of history had escaped me. More importantly, I was beginning to suspect that my antique boat had been unfairly blamed for an awful lot of spilled gravy.

Ellie Martin Cliffe For Taste Of Home.

According to Moore, traditional gravy boats were often intended to be used with small ladles, their handles resting nearly in the notch we’ve come to think of as a spout. In the sort of formal household familiar to anyone who’s watched The Gilded Age, a footman would have served the gravy or sauce by the spoonful rather than by tipping the entire boat over someone’s plate. It’s a rather elegant arrangement, and one that makes considerably more sense to me than trying to coax gravy out of a vessel that seems determined to spill all over the tablecloth.

According to recent reports, moore also offers an explanation for how we got into the habit of pouring. He says that around the middle of the 20th century, ceramic manufacturers began doing away with matching ladles to save money. Without the ladles, people started using the boats as little pitchers, and eventually the pouring method became familiar practice.

Of course, some gravy boats really were designed for pouring, and the presence of a spout doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve misunderstood the entire object. Both methods have a history, although I find Moore’s explanation fascinating. A piece of dishware I’ve used for years suddenly makes much more sense, and I rather like the possibility that I might accidentally stumble upon its matching ladle one day while I’m out treasure hunting.

Sources indicate that for gravy boats intended to be used with a ladle, the boat stays on the table while guests serve themselves by the spoonful. A small sauce or gravy ladle works perfectly well, even if it wasn’t made to match the boat, and its handle can rest against the spout if the shape allows.

This is especially useful for gravy boats with attached saucers, which can be awkward to tip without sending accumulated drips onto the table. As Etiquetteer notes, ladling sauce is traditional, but pouring is perfectly acceptable when there’s no ladle.

Sources indicate that and if your gravy boat pours beautifully, by all means carry on. Mine has never been especially cooperative, and after all these years, I’m rather pleased to discover that there may be a good explanation as to why.

#158849. Industry News: The Best Cold-Weather Cocktails to Drink This Holiday Season

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2068 w)

Industry News: The Best Cold-Weather Cocktails to Drink This Holiday Season

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2068 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I typically take a less-is-more approach when it comes to my beverage choices.
  • Sources indicate that what’s a cozy cocktail?
  • There are many paths a cold-weather cocktail may take.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I typically take a less-is-more approach when it comes to my beverage choices. Having been burned one too many times by the flavor-packed ‘ingenuity’ of a bar’s signature cocktail, I’ve come to the conclusion that a martini, Negroni, or gin and tonic are better suited to my spartan palate. But once the holidays roll around, well, my fidelity to simplicity goes out the window, and I am an enthusiastic proprietor of the cozy cocktail.

Sources indicate that what’s a cozy cocktail? Exactly what you think it is. A spirited sip that summons the mood of a crackling fireplace and the flavors of a Christmas kitchen. That transports you to a snowed-in cabin in Lapland, or a bustling holiday market in Germany. And I’m not talking about kitschy cocktails afflicted by crushed-up candy canes and artificial syrups—no, no. These are recipes that chase the outer limits of mixology, bringing together all that is merry and bright and elegantly transmuting it into your glass.

There are many paths a cold-weather cocktail may take. Traditional classics, like eggnog and hot toddies, are always welcome. For something theatrical, a smoked tipple does the trick (top marks for those performed tableside). For an off-the-charts cozy cocktail, those infused with seasonal spices will leave you deliriously jolly. And if you can’t bear to part ways with your old fashioned or espresso martini, take solace in knowing there are ways to ‘winter-fy’ these quintessential favorites.

In a recent development, if you’re ready to raise a glass of something cozy in the coming weeks, let the guide below inform your order. And for those who wish to whip up cocktails for a festive fête at home, don’t miss the recipes at the end. Bar carts at the ready!

It has been revealed that the holidays present a decadent array of creamy cocktails calibrated specifically for the season. Take eggnog, for example. This rich tipple originated from a hot, milky, ale-adjacent drink called ‘posset’ that was enjoyed during Britain’s medieval era. Somewhere along the timeline, eggs joined the party, and several hundred years later, we’ve arrived at our modern-day recipes that consist of milk, heavy whipping cream, sugar, eggs, and nutmeg (spiked with rum, bourbon, or brandy). A boozy holiday milkshake, if you like.

Industry observers note that over at Smithereens in the East Village, head bartender Jacob Dorman wanted to make an eggnog with their in-house label rum, but decided to do an egg flip variation to show the versatility of the rum. (For reference, the main difference between an egg flip and eggnog is that a traditional flip leaves the dairy out.) “People always think of rum as a tropical spirit, but it can be warming and comforting too,” Dorman claims. He uses a squash amaro for his flip, which “is like drinking pumpkin pie (in a good way).”.

According to recent reports, another creamy drink that foregoes the use of eggs is coquito. This Puerto Rican holiday cocktail typically uses coconut milk, cream of coconut, evaporated milk, sweetened condensed milk, vanilla extract, cinnamon, and ground nutmeg—spiked with rum. In a similar spirit, at The Wig Shop in Boston, beverage director Oscar Simoza is presently serving up a Venezuelan-inspired take on eggnog. It’s made with banana peel-infused rum, batido de cambur (ripe banana and milk), and arequipe (caramelized milk). Notes of anise and cinnamon, alongside a hint of amaro, come together for a cocktail that is sublimely silky.

The Brandy Alexander is another perennial classic. It’s made with brandy or cognac, dark crème de cacao, heavy cream, and freshly grated nutmeg for garnish. One of my favorite variations is at Bar Rêve in Cobble Hill. “Ours is an après-ski homage,” co-founder Victor Triebel says. They pair a base of cognac with a layer of Frangelico whipped cream, finished with freshly grated nutmeg. “There’s nothing more luxurious than a warming brandy cocktail to end the evening,” Triebel adds.

Recent findings suggest that during the chilliest months of the year, a cocktail encircled by fragrant smoke is just what the doctor ordered. Last winter, I found myself in the grand lobby of the Carlton Hotel St. Moritz, where drinks are served beside a stone fireplace and arrive via trolley cart. Their Piz Nair Mule—presented in a glass case—is inspired by a mountain that rises 3,057 meters above the Engadin Valley. Once the case is opened, a gentle cloud of smoke escapes, revealing the cocktail and miniature alpine landscape, complete with a moss-covered mountain and tiny mountaineers traversing the summit. The cocktail itself is a soothing blend of fresh thyme and rosemary, spicy ginger, and lime.

It has been revealed that if you can’t make it all the way to Switzerland this year, fret not, because San Ysidro Ranch in Montecito, California, has an entire menu dedicated to its tableside smoked cocktails. I’ve had the Smoking Pig Poke, which combines rye whiskey, averna, Luxardo maraschino, and a bacon-wrapped brandied cherry—all smoked with cherry wood. (They also serve cocktails smoked with oak, hickory, pecan, and pear woods—in case you’re picky about such things.) And if you’d like to impress your friends and try your hand at your own smoked cocktails, this smoke infuser would make an excellent holiday gift.

Industry observers note that distilling the holiday season’s rich baking spices into a cocktail is nothing short of alchemy. Cinnamon, nutmeg, clove, cardamom, allspice—each offers its own shade of warmth, and can be used as liquor infusions, spiced syrups, bitters, or simply garnishes.

At the newly opened Thai restaurant, Hommali, head bartender Patrick Cura created their Horchata Oolong cocktail, blending tequila, shochu, and sweet vermouth that’s been infused with oolong and umami bitters. “We torch a cinnamon stick over the glass for the garnish so you get an initial hit of baking spice at the first sip,” he shares. “It feels like a warm hug in a glass, which is particularly enjoyable when the temps start to drop.”.

Recent findings suggest that over at The Portrait Bar inside The Fifth Avenue Hotel, bar director Darryl Chan’s Marrakesh cocktail is inspired by the spice markets of Morocco. And further downtown at abcV in the Flatiron District, the Saffron Mylk rum cocktail is a blend of spices and saffron, heated with oat milk and honey, then finished with lashings of nutmeg. “The aroma from the nutmeg gives a wonderful warmth, with the heady spice evoking the holidays,” Chris Moore, director of beverage at Jean-Georges Restaurants, says.

It has been revealed that and if you’re searching for something a bit lighter, head for Williamsburg dive Shenanigans for their spiced vodka cran, featuring vodka, mulled wine with baking spices, lemon, and soda. (Starting December 2, Shenanigans will kick off their holiday pop-up serving festive cocktails through the fresh year—make haste.).

Sources indicate that while the holidays have spurred legendary cocktail creations aplenty, if you prefer to stick to what you know, look for seasonal riffs on the classics. Hot cocoa is a wonderful place to start. You can spike your beloved hot chocolate with everything from aged rum and bourbon to cointreau and Bailey’s Irish cream. At Limo Bar in the East Village, their Santa’s Coffee cocktail dials up the cozy by pairing Irish whiskey and coffee with maple syrup and salted maple cream.

In a recent development, on a recent visit to the newly opened Bar CC, I ordered the Vesuvio, which is their spin on a coffee Boulevardier. The cocktail layers coffee-infused bourbon with cacao, tonic bean, amontillado sherry, Barolo Chinato, Campari, and Cappelletti rosso. The cocktail is then clarified with heated milk that’s been enriched with mascarpone. (Professional mixology here; do not attempt at home.) But wait! I haven’t even arrived at the best part: an edible lace doily is delicately draped over the glass, resulting in the most elegant riff on a Boulevardier you or I have ever encountered.

For the espresso martini devout among us, head for Pinky Swear to order the Cloud 9, which is an espresso martini garnished with a torched marshmallow. Or if you’re an old fashioned fanatic, take note of the Outtake at New Orleans’s Cure bar, which is seasoned with warm walnut and crisp ginger. Even clear spirits can receive the holiday treatment—at Dandelion in the West Village, their Poire None cocktail swirls together tequila, mezcal, ginger, allspice, yellow Chartreuse, and pear cider for an autumnal riff on the timeless mule. And at Dean’s, rather than relying on brandy or whiskey to conjure the cozies, their winter-friendly take on a classic sbagliato features sloe gin and elderflower liqueur for a deeper, fruitier character.

When in doubt, if you have a go-to cocktail but want to get into the spirit of the season, ask your bartender what they’ve got up their sleeve.

Not drinking alcohol? There are plenty of cozy mocktails that still fit the prompt. Beverages like eggnog, coquito, hot toddies, and hot chocolate can all be created with as much depth and complexity as their boozy counterparts—just skip the liquor part at the end. The Pear of Aces at Golden Steer is an aromatic hot toddy that simmers whole cloves, cinnamon, and star anise with lush pear nectar and melted lemon sherbet.

Industry observers note that or there’s the spirit-free amaretto sour at The Lobby Bar inside Hotel Chelsea, which doubles down on roasted flavors. This cocktail uses a zero-proof Amaretto liqueur made of roasted almonds from Puglia, plus a roasted green tea that’s acidified with lemon juice. “The cocktail is served up with a floater of honey-miso whipped cream, to replicate the head of egg white foam from a traditional sour-style cocktail,” shares Brian Evans, the director of bars at Sunday Hospitality.

Throwing a holiday party and need a few cozy cocktail ideas? Continue below for libations that will get everyone into the spirit of the season.

Industry observers note that directions: Add all ingredients to a cocktail shaker and shake hard. Double strain into a coupe and garnish with grated chocolate.

“The Grasshopper is usually credited to Tujague's in New Orleans. It's a simple drink: crème de menthe, crème de cacao, and a splash of Franca menta and fresh cream, shaken until frothy and served a cool, pale green. Mint and chocolate taste like candy canes and peppermint bark, and the cream makes it smooth and soft. The green looks right at home by a tree or under twinkling lights. It's light and festive, a little nostalgic, and closer to dessert in a glass than to a cocktail” - Linden Pride, principal, Dante Elizabeth Street.

According to recent reports, directions: Run the apples through an extractor to separate the juice from the solids, letting the juice pour directly into a frothing pitcher. Add the sauce and bourbon. Steam all ingredients with a steam wand as though preparing milk for a latte. Pour into a heated mug.

Toddy Sauce Directions: Toast eight cinnamon sticks and four grams of whole black pepper in a pot. Add 650 grams Lambic (Duchess de Bourgogne), 650 grams Maple syrup, 12 grams turmeric and nine grams black pepper. Bring to a quick boil then lower to a simmer for 10 minutes. Cool and strain into a deli.

“Fresh pressed green apples are some of my favorite things to work with because the texture is so frothy coming out of the Breville. Steaming them doubles down on the intensity of the technique. The spice blend of turmeric, black pepper, and cinnamon evokes strong winter memories without falling into ‘pumpkin spice’ or Angostura bitters. Everything remains both familiar and impossibly fresh.” - Owen Gibler, Beverage Director, Bar Roza.

In a recent development, directions: Beat egg yolks and sugars until lightened in color and texture. In a separate bowl, combine dairy, spirits, salt, and nutmeg. Slowly stream the mixture into the beaten egg yolks and sugar while mixing. Once homogeneous, transfer to a sterile glass container and refrigerate for at least one week, ideally one month. Serve with freshly grated nutmeg.

“An elevated take on the holiday classic, Beckon’s Aged Eggnog is prepared months in advance, allowing bonded bourbon, Armagnac, aged and white rum to mellow alongside egg yolks, cream, milk, sugar and nutmeg. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

According to recent reports, do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

Industry observers note that while the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

According to recent reports, reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

A little ingenuity with an ordinary piece of silverware makes for a beautiful holiday cheese board.

Recent findings suggest that as much as I love a big, elaborate holiday dinner, I have a particular fondness for the hours leading up to it, when the wine has been opened and everyone is grazing around the kitchen. A good cheese board is almost always part of the festivities in my house. My affection for charcuterie boards is, admittedly, not doing much to challenge the millennial stereotype.

I love choosing cheeses and spreads that complement one another and bringing out some of my favorite serving pieces for the occasion. It’s one of the more enjoyable bits of prepping holiday party appetizers, in part because so much of the work can be done well before anyone arrives. And while I’m happy to devote a little extra time to the presentation, I’m always equally happy to discover a little shortcut that leaves me more time for the people I’m feeding.

One of my favorite recent discoveries is a clever trick for slicing cheese into neat, even pieces using the tines of an ordinary dinner fork. It’s the sort of kitchen trick that seems almost embarrassingly obvious once you’ve seen it.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

Rather than eyeballing the thickness of each slice, you can use the evenly spaced tines of a fork to mark the cheese beforehand, giving yourself a cutting guide.

It has been revealed that start with a wedge of cheese and gently press the tips of the fork’s tines into the face you’ll be cutting into, leaving a row of small, evenly spaced indentations. Repeat as needed across the back of the wedge, then use a sharp knife to slice between the marks. Having those little reference points makes it much easier to maintain a consistent thickness from one slice to the next.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

This trick is particularly well suited to cheeses like Gouda, cheddar and Gruyere, which are generally firm enough to slice cleanly but pliable enough to take the impression of a fork. I wouldn’t bother with a ripe Brie or a crumbly blue cheese, both of which lend themselves to a less structured presentation anyway.

I love this trick for fanning slices of cheese around the edge of a charcuterie board or arranging them in pretty, overlapping rows. And given the number of things competing for my attention when I’m entertaining, I’m delighted to delegate the finer points of cheese geometry to a fork.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

In a recent development, while orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

In a recent development, meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

It has been revealed that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

Add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

Is It Rude to Bring Your Own Food to Thanksgiving?

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before you show up with a casserole (or a bucket of KFC), here's what you need to know about Thanksgiving guest etiquette.
  • Thanksgiving is a holiday meant to bring people together, yet it has somehow become one of the more divisive days of the year.
  • Recent findings suggest that for the record, I say serve both kinds of cranberry sauce, get marshmallows off my sweet potatoes and we eat dinner whenever the host notes dinner is ready.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Before you show up with a casserole (or a bucket of KFC), here's what you need to know about Thanksgiving guest etiquette.

Thanksgiving is a holiday meant to bring people together, yet it has somehow become one of the more divisive days of the year. Do you serve canned cranberry sauce or get fresh cranberries to make one from scratch? Should sweet potatoes be combined with marshmallows? And what time are we eating dinner?

Recent findings suggest that for the record, I say serve both kinds of cranberry sauce, get marshmallows off my sweet potatoes and we eat dinner whenever the host notes dinner is ready. I can already feel the consternation boiling up if you disagree. But that is all part of the magic of the holiday!

I think it’s beautiful that no two families celebrate Thanksgiving the same way. Although, with all that preparation and planning, emotions can run high. It is very difficult to cook for large groups of people, and even more so when people have strong opinions about the meal. So if a guest brings their own food, is that considerate or rude? Should they bring enough to share or just what they want to eat?

As a food writer and frequent host, I am going to tell you how to navigate this etiquette dilemma.

Once upon a time, a member of my extended family brought KFC to my house because he did not like what my mom was cooking for dinner. This is undoubtedly rude and totally not OK. But it’s also a more extreme example of what people think of when they imagine “bringing your own food” somewhere.

According to recent reports, the short answer here is: no, it’s not OK to bring your own food to Thanksgiving dinner unless it has specifically been identified as a potluck-style meal. You can—and should!—ask the host if you can bring something, but if they say no, you need to respect that.

Sources indicate that A more realistic answer is probably it depends. I know, that’s kind of annoying. But I think this is a really nuanced question, and I want to do it justice. There really isn’t a one-size-fits-all answer. Here are some scenarios:.

Sources indicate that I’m sorry to break it to you, but this isn’t a real reason. It’s definitely a bummer, but sometimes that’s just how things go. Make some light-hearted jokes about it in the group chat with your cousins, and suck it up. This is one meal on one day, and it is not a good enough reason to bring your own food. Have a significant breakfast before heading over, and take very small portions. If anyone notices, a simple “I’m saving room for dessert” is a perfect get-out-of-jail-free card.

I suggest bringing appetizers or snacks instead of something for the main meal. Snacks are often overlooked when there is already a turkey in the oven and a pot on every burner. Tell the host you’re bringing a veggie tray and some chips and dips to snack on before the meal. Plus, it’s a separate thing and doesn’t really step on the host’s toes the way bringing an entire lasagna would.

First, know that I support you. But second, this is a you problem, and I think you know that. Load up on dinner rolls and volunteer to make a pot of coffee and do the dishes after the meal. It doesn’t have to be a major deal, and you can get back to regular food on Friday.

Sources indicate that this is the biggest exception and one that merits its own section. If you or members of your immediate family have food allergies, you can absolutely bring your own food—but it’s really vital to coordinate with the host. It shouldn’t feel like an ambush. Communicating to the host that you will be bringing gluten-free rolls or a dairy-free macaroni and cheese to ensure that you have something safe to eat is totally fine.

And I would argue that this is more relevant with kids than adults. It’s really important for kids to feel welcome in your home and to enjoy this holiday safely with all their family members. Anything you can do to alleviate stress or anxiety is not only good manners but also totally in the spirit of Thanksgiving.

In a recent development, it’s good guest etiquette to communicate with the host in advance. Once you receive the invite, volunteer to bring something. If you’re a champion baker, offer to make the pies or a nice, crusty sourdough loaf. You can even say you have a great Brussels sprouts recipe that’s been a hit with the family lately and you’d love to share it with more people. Or, simply ask if they would prefer a bottle of red or white wine.

Thanksgiving might be the most food-centric day of the year. But in my experience, the food becomes secondary as I sit around the table talking and laughing with my loved ones. There is always a moment where the stress melts away and I’m filled with an overwhelming sense of joy and gratitude. And that, my friends, is what the holiday is all about.

Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that there’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster.
  • Crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation.
  • For such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster. But chief among them is one whose very name promises something different, something with French sophistication and an air of mystery that demands a moniker all its own: crêpes Suzette.

Crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation. The drama comes from the flames—thin, traditional French crêpes are drenched in a sauce made of orange liqueur, which is then set ablaze (typically tableside in many restaurants), causing the spirits to simmer and the sugars to caramelize. French chef Andrea Calstier, of Michelin-starred La Bastide in North Salem, Upcoming York, grew up eating them with his family, and in the brasseries of his home country.

For such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare. And for such an iconic French dessert, well, it may not technically be French at all. So where did these flaming pancakes come from? Where did they go? And isn’t it about time we bring them back?

While there are conflicting reports about the original creator of crêpes Suzette, the top candidate is Henri Charpentier, chef at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, Monaco, in the late 1800s. But while multiple roads lead back to Charpentier, the path gets murky, contradicted by both general plausibility and Charpentier himself.

Originally, Charpentier claimed credit for the iconic dish in his autobiography, Life à la Henri: Being the Memoirs of Henri Charpentier. In this 1934 volume, he suggested that the dish was a happy accident, tinged with drama. He alleged that as a young man working at the Café de Paris, he had been carrying a platter of crêpes to the Prince of Wales (the future King Edward VII) and stepped too near a chafing dish, setting the crêpes on fire, to the shock and delight of the prince, who proposed naming the newly created dish after his dining companion, a young woman named Suzette. (Frustratingly little information is available on who this Suzette may have been, if she was a real person at all.).

The story has the right theatrical touches for the dish, but it is almost certainly apocryphal, not least because Charpentier himself, in an interview with American writer Elsie Lee for the 1950s “Compleat Imbiber” series, mentioned that he had developed the dish by taking a beloved childhood fruit crêpe and adding the then-fashionable touches of a liquor-based sauce and, presumably, a flame.

Wherever it came from, though, and whatever Charpentier had to say about it, Suzette’s unwitting legacy has endured for more than a century—her crêpes have remained a household name, even if they have fallen somewhat out of style. While chef Calstier notes that they’re still “served in many restaurants” in his native Marseille and that “French customers…are accustomed to seeing crêpes Suzette in any brasserie,” he admitted that “here in the U.S., they are more difficult to find.”.

It has been revealed that part of the reason may be that, as with many dishes that predate the Edwardian era, it simply went out of fashion. But according to Lucile Plaza, executive chef at Benoit Latest York, it’s a result of the dish’s inherent service requirements: “True tableside service requires high staffing levels and precise choreography that a busy modern kitchen can’t always support daily,” she states. In London’s West End, fine-dining heavyweights Savoy Grill and The Ritz take this showmanship to the extreme, with portable burners and bottles of Grand Marnier on wooden trolleys.

Sources indicate that but while there are complications to adding an edible spectacle to a restaurant menu, there are benefits, too. Chef Plaza notes that for the kitchen, “Suzette is brilliant because it is the ultimate way to use leftover crêpes. The intense bathing in the hot, rich citrus sauce revives the starch perfectly.” But not every restaurant that serves crêpes Suzette does so with a tableside flourish: In London’s St. John’s Wood, Oslo Court Restaurant, which is famous for its retro menu of classics like steak Diane and sole Veronique (two more of Edward VII's girlfriends, perhaps?), crêpes Suzette are brûléed with a torch in the kitchen rather than set aflame at the table. Adding crêpes Suzette to a menu may only be as hard as a restaurant wants it to be.

According to recent reports, A burst of blue-tinged flame may not be necessary for the dish to achieve its signature caramelization, but it is key to the show—and a major point in favor of the dish’s present-day revival. As the old saying goes, “we eat with our eyes first,” and it’s truer than ever today. In fact, for many diners in the age of social media, it’s the phone that eats first, and that’s where crêpes Suzette has real potential for a modern renaissance. Nearly 400,000 viewers have watched a YouTube video of the tableside crêpes Suzette service at the London Ritz, and more than a million have viewed a TikTok of crêpes Suzette being prepared tableside at Switzerland’s five-star Suvretta House in Saint Moritz.

Sources indicate that spectacle is cool again, and whether dining out or cooking at home, we want to feel astonished and excited by the foods we eat. While a tableside flambé may prove logistically complicated at a restaurant scale, the feat is significantly easier to pull off at home—all it takes is a lighter or a match and a little confidence. Chef Calstier, for one, claims that crêpes Suzette are a favorite of his wife, Elena, adding, “You can prepare everything in advance and do the flambé in front of your guests to wow them.” Plus, he says, “they don’t require many ingredients, beyond that bottle of Grand Marnier that we all have stashed away somewhere. They’re quite simple to make.”.

Moreover, as delectable as classic crêpes Suzette are, they lend themselves well to fresh takes and customizations. Chef Plaza’s version at Benoit has a cherry twist: “Replacing Grand Marnier with kirsch is a natural match,” she notes. “The dry cherry distillate brings an incredible aroma to the tableside without adding cloying sugar.” Meanwhile, at La Bastide, chef Calstier dishes up a twist that uses French toast instead of crêpes while sticking to the classic flavors and flambé. We asked one of our favorite pastry chefs, Caroline Schiff, author of Daily Desserts: Treats on Repeat, to develop a savory version for us, which she describes as “a cheeky little twist” on the classic. In her take, inspired by French onion soup, crêpes layered with caramelized onions and nutty gruyère are set ablaze with a splash of sherry. “They are at once a novelty and a nod to the classic,” she says.

Charpentier, one imagines, would approve.

Giant Sheet-Pan Chocolate Almond Croissant

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant has a filling of frangipane and melted chocolate chips between two light, buttery sheets of puff pastry.
  • It has been revealed that this giant croissant is practically the size of a sheet pan.
  • According to recent reports, preheat the oven to 425°F.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Our giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant has a filling of frangipane and melted chocolate chips between two light, buttery sheets of puff pastry.

It has been revealed that this giant croissant is practically the size of a sheet pan. The bigger, the better, as they say, but we’re more into its shareable nature and simple-to-make design. Shatteringly crisp puff pastry (store-bought, of course) replaces hard-to-make croissant dough, with extra square footage for both this treat’s iconic croissant fillings: pain au chocolat and almond croissant. Win-win-win. Save this giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant for special occasions or holiday mornings.

According to recent reports, preheat the oven to 425°F. On a lightly floured surface, roll out each sheet of puff pastry to a 12×10-inch rectangle. Place one on a parchment-lined 15x10x1-inch baking pan. Top the puff pastry with a second piece of parchment paper and a second 15x10x1-inch baking pan. This keeps the puff pastry from rising too much so it stays flat.

Industry observers note that bake the puff pastry for 15 minutes. Remove the top pan and parchment. Continue baking the puff pastry until it’s golden brown, five to seven minutes longer. Cool the puff pastry on a wire rack. Repeat the same process with the second slice of puff pastry.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, in a small bowl, beat together the softened butter, almond flour and confectioners’ sugar until they’re light and fluffy, two to three minutes. Add the egg and beat well until it’s incorporated.

Place one baked sheet of puff pastry on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Spread two-thirds of the almond filling over it.

Sprinkle the chocolate chips evenly all over. Carefully place the second sheet of baked puff pastry over top, and pipe or spread the remaining third of the almond filling on top.

Sprinkle the top with sliced almonds.

Reduce the oven setting to 350°. Bake the croissant just until the filling is set, 18 to 20 minutes longer. Cool the croissant completely on a wire rack before serving.

Just as you’re ready to serve, dust the top with confectioners’ sugar and, if desired, drizzle it with warm hot fudge.

Store leftover giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant in an airtight container in the fridge. It can be kept for up to three days. Just know that it is best enjoyed the day of, as the frangipane will make the puff pastry soggy.

It has been revealed that yes, you can make certain aspects of a giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant ahead of time, but wait to assemble and bake it until you’re ready to serve. You can bake the puff pastry sheets one day ahead, let them cool to room temperature, wrap them tightly in storage wrap and store them at room temperature. Make the frangipane up to two days beforehand and keep it covered in the fridge.

Yes, you can make a gluten-free version of this giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant. Simply replace the puff pastry with a gluten-free variety. DuFour, Sweet Loren’s and Schar make fantastic gluten-free puff pastry. All other ingredients are naturally gluten free (but do double-check the hot fudge, if you’re using it); just make sure they weren’t processed in a facility that handles wheat.

In a recent development, serve your giant sheet-pan chocolate almond croissant with strong coffee or tea. Pair it with other brunch, like egg casseroles, plates of bacon and sausage and a fruit salad. I wouldn’t set out any other sweets—this croissant is plenty!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

Recent findings suggest that the rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s key that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

Sources indicate that most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Sources indicate that preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

Sources indicate that while potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

Mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I thought I knew exactly how I felt about ranch dressing.
  • I’ve never been particularly fond of ranch dressing.
  • Recent findings suggest that I suspect my aversion began during childhood, watching my friends dunk perfectly good slices of pizza into enormous puddles of cheap ranch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

I thought I knew exactly how I felt about ranch dressing. Then I made Ina's version.

I have a confession to make. I’ve never been particularly fond of ranch dressing. I realize this puts me at odds with a substantial portion of the American population, but I’ve always preferred a good balsamic vinaigrette or a creamy Caesar. And despite making countless salad dressings over the years, I’ve never once felt compelled to make ranch.

Recent findings suggest that I suspect my aversion began during childhood, watching my friends dunk perfectly good slices of pizza into enormous puddles of cheap ranch. I found the whole business unappealing, an opinion that has apparently skipped a generation seeing as both of my children now do exactly the same thing. There’s always a bottle of ranch in our refrigerator that was purchased specifically for pizza night, and it has absolutely nothing to do with me.

Industry observers note that then I came across an Instagram reel of Ina Garten making her buttermilk ranch dressing for a wedge salad. I’ve trusted Ina with everything from roast chicken to panna cotta, and if anyone could persuade me to reconsider my longstanding position on ranch, I figured it would be her. So, after decades of avoiding it, I finally made a batch of ranch dressing.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

Sources indicate that ina’s recipe makes about 3 cups of dressing, which initially struck me as an ambitious quantity for someone with my history of distatte. Fortunately, it comes together in just a few minutes, and the ingredients are far more fresh and interesting than anything I’d previously associated with ranch.

Combine the scallions, basil, lemon juice, Dijon mustard, olive oil, garlic, salt and pepper in a food processor fitted with a steel blade. Puree them for 15 to 20 seconds, until the mixture is smooth.

Industry observers note that add the mayonnaise, Greek yogurt and buttermilk, then blend the dressing again until everything is thoroughly combined. Transfer the dressing to a covered container and refrigerate it for an hour to let the flavors develop.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

That’s really all there is to it. No complicated technique or careful emulsifying, and very little cleanup. The hour in the refrigerator is important, though, since it gives the garlic, herbs and other seasonings time to mingle with the creamy ingredients.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

Of course, I expected Ina’s ranch to be better than the bottled varieties I’ve tried. What I didn’t expect was for it to taste like an entirely different dressing.

In a recent development, the first thing that struck me was how fresh it was. The basil and scallions give it a wonderful, almost garden-like quality, while the garlic and Dijon add savory sharpness that keeps all that creaminess interesting. There’s plenty of richness from the mayonnaise, but the buttermilk, Greek yogurt and lemon juice provide enough acidity to balance it. It’s tangy, herbaceous and wonderfully flavorful—without the heavy, slightly cloying quality I’ve always associated with ranch.

And the basil! It’s not an herb I would have thought to put in ranch dressing, but it works beautifully. Its flavor comes through clearly without overwhelming the other ingredients, giving the dressing a character all its own.

In her video, Ina serves the dressing over a wedge salad topped with tomatoes and onion. Having already entrusted her with the dressing, I figured I might as well follow her lead with the salad, too. I made my own wedge with Flavor Bombs tomatoes (my favorites), pepitas and crispy pieces of bacon, then spooned a generous amount of ranch over the whole thing. The cold, crunchy lettuce was the perfect backdrop for the dressing, while the sweet tomatoes, salty bacon and nutty pepitas made the whole thing particularly satisfying. I’ve always loved a good wedge salad, but this was easily one of the best I’ve had.

Industry observers note that by the time I’d finished testing and photographing the recipe, nearly half the dressing was gone, and I was already making plans for the rest. I have to admit, I’m even curious to see how it tastes with pizza, which is not something I ever expected to say about ranch dressing.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Industry observers note that no ricotta? Reach for a scoop of protein-rich cottage cheese. It's the secret to these tender, moist and protein-rich meatballs.

My kids have never been huge meat eaters. In fact, my son is more likely to polish off a giant bowl of cherry tomatoes than he is to dig into a burger. Meatballs, though, have always been the exception—and these cottage cheese meatballs have been a long-time favorite. My kids love how tender and juicy they are, and I love that they sneak a little extra protein into their diet.

Many traditional meatball recipes already include ricotta cheese, which binds and adds moisture to the meat mixture. Cottage cheese is a natural swap, adding fat that keeps the meatballs irresistibly moist and tender. Once these protein-packed meatballs are simmered in your favorite jarred pasta sauce and served over pasta, people will never guess that cottage cheese is the secret ingredient.

Industry observers note that editor’s Tip: For the softest, most tender meatballs, handle them gently as you shape them. Avoid overhandling or compacting the meat too much (one of Grandma’s best meatball tips), as it can make the meatballs tough and dense.

Ellie Crowley FOr Taste Of Home.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Hold the jelly! The iconic peanut butter brand is taking a surprisingly savory direction with its latest product.

Who notes peanut butter doesn’t deserve a spot in your dinner rotation?

Industry observers note that jif, the beloved peanut butter brand that’s been a staple in American pantries for decades, has ventured into some unexpected territory. If you’re a frequent Costco shopper, you might want to take a closer look the next time you’re browsing the instant noodles.

Some locations of the warehouse retailer are now carrying a six-pack of Jif stir-fry-style instant ramen noodles, giving shoppers an entirely different way to enjoy the taste of peanut butter.

But so far, the reviews among shoppers are mixed.

In a recent development, “Anyone who thinks this sounds gross has never had Thai food and it reveals. Peanut butter noodles are kinda awesome,” one fan wrote in a video making the rounds on Instagram.

“Prolly fire w some chili oil,” another claimed.

Sources indicate that “I had this last month. Pretty good for instant noodles,” another said.

A fourth wrote, “As a peanut butter [connoisseur] I don’t approve this.”.

“Diabolical waste of resources,” a fifth claimed.

Industry observers note that peanuts have long been incorporated into savory noodle dishes, particularly in Asian-inspired cooking. Still, seeing the recognizable Jif logo on a package of instant noodles might have you raising your eyebrows. Rather than replicating the sweet, creamy taste of a spoonful of peanut butter, the noodles take a more savory approach. The seasoning contains peanut flour alongside ingredients like soy sauce, garlic and artificial beef flavor.

Jif has another product worth keeping an eye out for at Costco. The brand’s peanut butter and chocolate pretzel Snappers hit shelves in October and offer a sweet-and-salty alternative for those who aren’t quite sold on the noodles.

Industry observers note that as always, product availability can vary by warehouse, so it’s worth checking your warehouse’s stock online before making a special trip. You can also buy the Jif instant ramen at Walmart or Amazon.

But the real question is, would you give peanut butter ramen a try, or is this one food crossover you’ll happily sit out?

Industry observers note that this chocolate mousse cake ticks a lot of boxes—major, grand, ideal for the holidays, and just enough of a challenge to ensure you feel accomplished. The one-bowl chocolate cake layer is dense and deeply fudgy; the mousse is airy and light; and the thin slip of ganache on top brings it all together. No matter what kind of year you’ve had, this dessert is the way to cap it all off.

Sources indicate that making the mousse alone will teach you three foundational pastry techniques, and they’re all hidden in plain sight. It starts with a crème anglaise; adding that to chopped chocolate yields a crémeux, and folding in whipped cream turns it into a mousse. Magical. The cake can be easily made from start to finish in the space of a morning, but can be split up further to fit your schedule. Bake the chocolate cake layer and chop all the chocolate on the first day; make the mousse and assemble the cake the following.

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 6 hours for chilling).

It has been revealed that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lay a sheet of parchment paper over base of pan. Fit band on top and clamp shut to hold parchment in place; scrunch up around base. Wrap a sheet of foil around bottom and up sides of pan (this will help prevent any leaking).

Whisk together 1 cup (125 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, ⅓ cup (28 g) Dutch-process cocoa powder, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking soda in a medium bowl. Add 1 large egg, ⅓ cup buttermilk, ⅓ cup vegetable oil, 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and ½ cup water and whisk until smooth, about 1 minute. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out with a few moist crumbs attached and top springs back when gently pressed, 25–35 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 10 minutes. Remove band from base; slide cake off parchment and base and onto rack. Let cool completely; discard parchment and foil.

Sources indicate that do Ahead: Cake can be baked 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

Sources indicate that place 10.5 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a large heatproof bowl. Bring 1 cup whole milk to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium, about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, vigorously whisk 4 large egg yolks and ½ cup (100 g) sugar in a small heatproof bowl until smooth and lemon yellow, about 1 minute.

Gradually stream hot milk into yolk mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Return to pan, scraping bowl clean with a heatproof rubber spatula. Cook over medium, stirring constantly, until thickened just enough to coat a spoon, about 5 minutes. (Do not let custard come to a boil or it will curdle.) Immediately pour over chocolate; let sit 1 minute. Add 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and whisk vigorously until chocolate is melted and crémeux is smooth.

Beat 1¾ cups heavy cream in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until soft peaks form, about 5 minutes. Add one quarter of whipped cream to crémeux; mix until combined (this will lighten it). Add remaining whipped cream in 3 additions, gently folding after each until incorporated before adding more.

It has been revealed that reassemble springform pan; line bottom with a parchment paper round. Wrap a strip of parchment around inside of pan to create a collar that stands about 1" above band (ends should overlap by at least 3"). Using a large serrated knife, trim off mound on top of cake to create a flat surface if needed. Return cake to pan. Spoon mousse over and smooth into an even layer with an offset spatula or spoon. Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet; chill until top of mousse feels set, about 2 hours.

It has been revealed that place 4 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a medium heatproof bowl. Bring ½ cup heavy cream and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt to a bare simmer in a small saucepan over medium. Pour over chocolate and let sit 2 minutes. Whisk gently until smooth. If ganache feels hot, let cool until lukewarm but still pourable, 8–10 minutes.

According to recent reports, pour ganache over mousse and smooth with offset spatula. Chill until mousse is completely set (ganache will set in about 30 minutes), at least 4 hours and up to 12 hours (no need to cover unless fridge has other strong smells).

It has been revealed that to serve, remove band from base and peel parchment strip away from sides of cake. Transfer cake with base to a plate and let sit 20 minutes; sprinkle top with flaky sea salt.

According to recent reports, whenever Burger King drops a newly introduced limited-edition themed menu, I basically grab my keys and head out the door. Yes, it is that serious! I was lucky to grab a King Jr. Meal with a Hello Kitty toy the day before my local BK sold out of them completely. If you like collectibles, I’m sure you feel the same way.

It has been revealed that between last year’s Spongebob Meal and this year’s Mandolorian Meal, I have been really happy with all the new food drops from Burger King. I dream of eating a Whopper off of a square yellow bun again. So when I saw that Burger King will have a limited-edition Peanuts Holiday Meal this year, I cleared my schedule for the day the meal drops. Here’s everything you need to know about the festive new menu. Good grief!

It has been revealed that the star of the collaboration is the Peanuts Pack, a holiday feast served in a collectible Snoopy Doghouse Box. But the packaging isn’t the only fun surprise: Each Peanuts Pack also comes with one of two exclusive Snoopy holiday beanies. Talk about a cute way to top off your meal!

In a recent development, for the main course, guests can choose between a flame-grilled Whopper with cheese or a 10-piece order of chicken nuggets. The nuggets come with a latest Woodstock Golden Ranch dipping sauce, which I can’t wait to try.

Here are the other fresh treats that come in the meal:.

The Peanuts King Jr. Meal comes in its own Snoopy Doghouse Box and includes a choice of hamburger, cheeseburger or four-piece chicken nuggets. Kids can pick applesauce or french fries for a side, along with milk or apple juice. The best part? ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
